speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: TABLING OF SOVIET NOTE AND CANADIAN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 4 I informed the house that on March 2 a note addressed to the government of Canada by the Soviet government had been received, concerning the possibility of negotiations taking place on problems connected with or relating to Germany. This Soviet note did not contain anything of significance which was not to be found in the notes which were addressed on the same date to the United Kingdom, the United States and France.
The Canadian government in its reply to the Soviet note, which reply was given on April 24, expressed support for the proposals put forward by the western powers, and accepted by the Soviet government, which would lead shortly to negotiations in Geneva at the level of foreign ministers. The note stated that in view of the imminence of these negotiations the Canadian government did not consider it would be of value to comment in detail on the matters raised in the Soviet note. The hope was expressed, however, that the Soviet government will treat the coming negotiations as a real opportunity to achieve a lessening of international tension, and to settle some of the pressing problems on a basis that will take into account the legitimate interests of all concerned.
For the information of the house I should like to table copies of the Soviet note and the Canadian reply.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF SOVIET NOTE AND CANADIAN REPLY
speechtext: I am sure the house will welcome the tabling of these documents by the Prime Minister. Can the Prime Minister say whether or not the Canadian reply in any way dealt with the latest proposal put forward by Her Majesty's government with regard to the new proposal for inspection, and if not, can the Prime Minister say whether or not Canada has been made aware of this proposal?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: TABLING OF SOVIET NOTE AND CANADIAN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in general the note dealt with the matters set out in the Soviet note. With respect to the other matter raised by the hon. member for Essex East, I wish to say that the Soviet union, we
regret, has not accepted the recent proposal. I take it what the hon. member has in mind is the proposal of the United States consolidating the progress so far made at Geneva?

subsubtopic: TABLING OF SOVIET NOTE AND CANADIAN REPLY
speechtext: I was referring to the latest proposal announced over the week end by the Prime Minister, with regard to the occasions when inspection teams would proceed into the territory of the countries concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: TABLING OF SOVIET NOTE AND CANADIAN REPLY
speechtext: In so far as that matter is concerned naturally-it was not delivered until Friday night-our reply did not deal with that particular phase. I thought the hon. member had in mind particularly the situation respecting the consolidation of progress already made in connection with nuclear tests.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF SOVIET NOTE AND CANADIAN REPLY
speechtext: Can the Prime Minister answer the other part of my question, which was whether or not Canada has received an intimation from Her Majesty's government about this new proposal, and is the Prime Minister in a position to make any comment in regard to it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: TABLING OF SOVIET NOTE AND CANADIAN REPLY
speechtext:
In so far as the first part of the question is concerned, naturally there has been information given.
With respect to the latter part of the question, I think the representations in general are acceptable and indeed offer a new vista of hope for a solution of the problem provided, of course, that these views are accepted, even in part, by the Soviet union when the foreign ministers' conference takes place on May 11.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF SOVIET NOTE AND CANADIAN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the members of this group are interested in the Prime Minister's statement. We welcome his tabling of these very interesting documents. As a party we are interested in a continuance of negotiations to the end that progress can be made toward peace in the world. We shall peruse these documents with interest.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare if he could give the house a report on the civil defence conference with the provinces which took place last Friday.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteiih (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CONFERENCE WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of her intention to ask this question. I might point out that all provincial governments, with the exception of Prince Edward Island, were represented by at least one minister and one or more officials. The federal government was represented by the
Inquiries of the Ministry Prime Minister, who addressed the conference at the morning session and stressed the need for decisive action in the field of civil defence, by the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Justice and myself, and for part of the time by the Minister of Defence Production and the two Ministers without Portfolio.
The purpose of the conference was to discuss with the provinces the proposed allocation of certain federal functions to national defence, to national health and welfare, to the R.C.M.P. and the emergency measures organization in the privy council office, and to obtain their views on the responsibilities which it is proposed to leave in provincial and local hands with increased federal technical and advisory services, as well as greater financial assistance. The allocation of the federal responsibilities was discussed with the provinces in considerable detail, and I can say to the house without reservation that in their broad outlines these new arrangements appealed to the provinces as being sensible and reasonable in every way.
We also discussed with the provinces the areas of responsibility which will remain in their hands and those of the municipal or regional civil defence organizations maintained under provincial direction. I think I can say that provincial reactions to all features of the federal proposals were favourable; particularly to the federal government's offer to increase the federal contribution to approved or local civil defence projects from 50 per cent, where this now applies, to 75 per cent.
Provincial ministers will now discuss these various questions with their colleagues, and we hope to have the official reactions of their governments at an early date. In the meantime it is the government's intention to proceed with the reallocation of purely federal functions to the departments and agencies I have mentioned.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Labour, which provides him with an opportunity to be a star performer this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: EFFECTS ON EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I wish to thank the hon. member for Kootenay West for having given me notice of this question. I am informed that on Thursday morning one of the officers on duty in the psychiatric ward of Kingston penitentiary was stabbed in the back by an inmate who was himself a patient in that ward. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he has any further information to give to the house with regard to the statement which he made last week in reply to my question on nuclear testing.

The hon. gentleman advised me of his intention to ask this question, and I might perhaps answer it by referring to the progress being made at Geneva, which indicates that there is little hope of the Soviet union agreeing to the cessation of nuclear tests in the atmosphere up to a height of 30 miles and the establishment of a control system to verify compliance with the agreement.

speechtext: I have a question I should like to direct to the Prime Minister, and I have sent him notice. Has the attention of the Prime Minister been drawn to an article in the April 25 edition of the Financial Post to the effect that the premier of British Columbia is intending to trade a portion of northern British Columbia to the United States in exchange for a corridor through the Alaska panhandle? If so, will he comment on this report?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORTED EXCHANGE OF LAND WITH U.S. FOR PANHANDLE CORRIDOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman sent me the clippings in question, and from an examination it appears to me that the status of the matter as reported in the press is that a member of the legislature of British Columbia has made a statement; but there is no indication, as I read it, that any attention is going to be given to the matter until the return of the premier of British Columbia from his vacation.
As the house knows, there are a number of bills on this general subject before the United States congress. One of these, I understand, would authorize the leasing on long term to Canada of a corridor through the Alaska panhandle. It is not considered very likely that the bill will be passed.
With regard to the general question of whether British Columbia is constitutionally capable of entering into an exchange arrangement, without expressing a legal viewpoint on the matter, not having consulted the law officers of the crown, I must say that I do express unequivocal doubts as to the constitutionality of such a move.

At the opening of the house on Friday morning the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) sought to move the adjournment of the house to discuss a matter
Monetary Policy
of urgent public importance, namely the announcement made the day before of an increase in the Bank of Canada rediscount rate to an unprecedented 4.9 per cent.

However, in view of the argument which has been advanced I suggest that every opportunity will be given on Monday. We will certainly provide a motion to go into supply, so the argument advanced by the hon. member for Laurier is met.
