speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Again on a question of privilege. Mr. Speaker, may I say that the hon. member is omitting to read the last sentence of the statement by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) on page 3013, which says:
-since he has suggested that we have a supply motion on Monday with this very kind of amendment under discussion.

I rise on a point of order. This intervention by the Minister of Public Works now is not in order. The hon. gentleman is making a speech, and these interruptions are certainly outside the rules of this house.

I take it that it will surprise no one when I say that I take a somewhat different approach to this matter from that taken by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I think that is a reasonable assumption, and surely the Minister of Public Works will not argue that is out of order, or raise another question of privilege. While our grievance, as I say, includes the subject matter sought to be raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia on Friday, it is on wider and somewhat different grounds. The motion I propose to move at the close of my remarks will however give that hon. member ample scope for the observations he may wish to make.
What I propose to do is to ask the house to express its regret at the ill-conceived and irresponsible action of the government in the field of debt management and monetary policy. We believe that these ill-conceived and irresponsible actions have had many unfortunate consequences for the Canadian people. One of those consequences, of course, is to be found in the rise, since the budget debate was concluded, in the bank rate to an unprecedented 4.97 per cent on April 23. This is the matter the hon. member for Assiniboia sought to raise on Friday.
However, as I said, that is only one of the unfortunate circumstances of the management, or perhaps I should say mismanagement, by the present government of its monetary policies. Perhaps I should say something at the very outset, in developing this subject, about the biggest operation of all in debt management in the past year, or since the present government came into office; that is the conversion loan. I should say something about the errors in concept and the inequities associated with that refunding operation. It will be recalled that the conversion loan was undertaken to replace the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth and ninth victory loans which were to mature in January, 1959; June, 1960; February, 1962; October, 1963, and September, 1966.
It will be recalled further that all these victory loans bore interest at the rate of 3

per cent per annum. With the exception of a right which holders of the fifth and sixth victory loan bonds had to subscribe for a new short term issue maturing in December, 1961, at 3 per cent, the new bonds were to mature in 1965, 1972 and 1983, and they were to bear interest at 3| per cent; 4J per cent; and 4J per cent, respectively.
In the first place the minister, in explaining the inclusion of these victory loans in his refinancing plan, dealt with maturities and pointed out that there was a call feature included in the 'last three issues. He argued from that fact, if I understood him correctly, that the maturities did not really extend up to eight years but rather, for all practical purposes, should be considered as three years. Well, that was, as I have said, his reason for including the last three victory loans, the seventh, eighth and ninth; and it was wrong. There was an error in calculation on his part in assuming that any investor would consider the maturity of those loans as all coming within three years; in other words, in assuming that any investor would consider that those bonds would be called at the end of three years.
He explained that interest rates were rising. At the same time, in making that explanation he was trying to suggest that the government would withdraw from circulation bonds which bore the lower rate of interest, namely 3 per cent. No investor would expect that to happen. No prudent government would do it unless there was some other very substantial reason for doing it. Therefore he was wrong in his assumption that the investor would assume that those bonds had an effective term of only three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the assessment the market puts on them.

I am just arguing the point; I am trying to interpret the minister very accurately and carefully. I have checked his speeches. In any event, there was a very easy way of removing that doubt and fear from the investors' minds. Since the minister knew the current interest rate was higher, he could have removed the fear by the simple announcement that he did not propose to call those bonds, that the government was not going to call those bonds. We would then be in the position where the bonds would mature on the dates indicated on the bonds. The minister's treatment of them on any other basis was quite wrong. It could easily have been corrected by that simple announcement on his part. That was the first serious error the minister made concerning the conversion operation.
Then, of course, in connection with the conversion operation there is the whole matter
Monetary Policy
of cost. I hope the minister will follow these figures; I think I have taken them accurately from his own statements. It will be recalled that the conversion loan cost by way of cash adjustments the sum of $42,500,000; by way of issuing fees the sum of $7 million; by way of commission to sales agents the sum of $20 million; by way of advertising the sum of $1,500,000, and by way of administrative costs the sum of $1,225,000. It will be recalled also that the added annual interest charge on the moneys being borrowed is in those early years some $58 million; that is by way of added interest charge alone. In addition to this additional interest charge there is the additional annual amortization charge. I admit a little confusion in getting what that is from the minister's figures, but I take it to be approximately $7,500,000. In other words the cost in added annual charges is something of the order of $65 million a year.
To show how needless part of this added cost was I should like to point out one feature pertaining to the ninth victory loan. If it had not been converted but had been left to carry on until maturity in the ordinary way, the interest charges saved on this portion of the national debt borrowings would have been $165 million; that is, $165 million in interest alone less than the amount the government agreed to pay by reconverting that issue. This is to me an enormous sum of money to add to the tax structure of this country, to put as a burden on the taxpayers because of the mistake in judgment of the Minister of Finance in including this victory loan in the conversion operation.
I am aware that the interest rates were rising at the time the conversion loan was undertaken. I do not for a minute deny that they were rising here and in the United States, but this question remains open to be settled. In my view there is no doubt at all but that some part of this increase in the interest charge is the minister's own responsibility, due to his failure to adopt proper monetary policies and in the general budgetary field since he took office in June of 1957. This raises the interesting point as to whether or not the minister should have undertaken the conversion loan at the time he did; or, indeed, if he was going to undertake it then, surely he owed a duty to the country and to the taxpayers to have more appreciation of the part his own responsibility as Minister of Finance and his own actions as Minister of Finance would have on the interest rate. That is particularly true as far as it pertains to his management of the national accounts.
306S

Monetary Policy
He may well ask-perhaps he will not argue it-how did his actions have any bearing on the rise in interest rates? They certainly did, because you go back in these things to what seems to be one prime factor, namely the confidence of the investing public in his administration. I cannot help but recall to his mind now the impact of his failure to deliver a budget in the first parliament in which he had any responsibility as Minister of Finance, his complete failure to deliver any budget during that whole parliament when the Conservative party was assuming office for the first time in 22 years. He would not express his views on monetary policy, or expound his views as to the national accounts and what should be done with respect to these matters. That undoubtedly did much to destroy the confidence of investors in Canadian government securities.
Perhaps I need not pursue this, but I can follow through with his actions time after time in the almost two years during which he has had the responsibility of Minister of Finance. Indeed, in this I do not wish to single out the Minister of Finance only. It is a responsibility that must be shared by his colleagues in other departments with respect to these budgetary and financial matters.
There is another interesting facet to this. There is the whole attitude of neglect of this subject by the present government. For some reason, which I for my part have never been able to understand, the Tories seem to regard this subject as not worthy of the most serious attention. They treat it as if it was something less than a very big and difficult subject confronting them. As an illustration of that I would draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that in the budget of 1958 the minister devoted a good deal of his time to the subject of debt management, with no inkling of what was coming. Just after that he switched quite suddenly from anything he had said on the subject of debt management and announced a conversion loan. It was to be on such a scale that he used on one occasion the term "gigantic"; in any case, it was to be very large. The lack of confidence in government bonds has been contributed to in large measure by the government's own actions and by the continuing prospect under the present government of successive deficits.
There is another feature about the high interest charges on such a large operation as the conversion loan, and that is that it has saddled this country with a base interest rate of some 44 per cent for the next 25 years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What does the hon. member mean by a base rate? The hon. member does not mean it is an average rate?

No, I do not suggest an average rate. I mean the government, having undertaken such a large conversion operation in issuing these long term bonds at a 44 per cent interest rate, if it was unnecessary to do it on such a large scale at that rate, or if that rate was contributed to by the government's own actions in its management of related matters, then it has the effect of making it difficult for governments to borrow easily below that rate within that term. It does tend, I think you will agree, to raise the whole basis on which government borrowings will be carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman be a little more fair and relate the interest rate to the maturity in question? A 25-year maturity in these circumstances is not comparable with a shorter maturity.

I do not see that is differing in fact from anything I am stating. The minister's point is not a point of order or of privilege. If the minister wants to argue that he will have his opportunity to do so. In the meantime it is my argument. These things are somewhat technical, and if I make any error in factual matters at any point I am happy to have him interrupt me; otherwise I do not think he should interrupt just for the purpose of stating an argument he may wish to advance.
There is another serious error in this whole conversion loan operation, and that is the effect of the government's policy in having the Bank of Canada undertake to buy the victory loan bonds at par; that is, at the time the conversion was being undertaken. It will be recalled that this whole operation was undertaken when the New York bond market had gone down sharply, or was in the process of going down, and the Canadian market was following in the same general trend. The government, in my view, made a serious error in establishing an artificial market for the victory loan bonds which it was seeking to convert. The creation of this artificial market at that time had very serious repercussions, and I will seek to develop those later in my argument. As a result, great numbers of holders of victory loan bonds did not convert their bonds into the new bonds but sold them for cash, and by that method took what I think I can show was a windfall capital profit of a very sizable nature. In some cases I guess it was five or six points, but a very substantial matter. That was made possible by the action of the government, and it was really in effect a capital bonus to those persons who were astute enough to see what the government's policy was. It was a bonus to those persons

who did not contribute to achieving the objective of the conversion operation.
Then during the operation another facet was that the Bank of Canada, by purchasing these bonds from individual holders, did so at prices, as I have said, higher than those which had been prevailing in the market, in fact at prices which were fairly sharply higher. It was a purely artificial level which applied to these victory bond holders. At the same time the government was attracting the savings of other less experienced Canadians who, due to the pressure of the campaign, were induced to invest their savings in government bonds at prices which subsequently have been shown to bear no relation to the real market value, because they were held above the real value by this artificial means. These people who took the windfall I have spoken about can now buy the new bonds under the conversion loan at a much lower rate, and they have been put in that position by not answering the appeal of the government in this very important matter.
Now, how many Canadians, under the urging of the advertising campaign and other propaganda used and paid for by the government, bought these higher interest bearing bonds at par? Unfortunately some of them have gone down as low as $92.50; they are down very low. It seems to me on that account alone that the government should indeed have a very bad conscience in having placed these artificially high values on the bonds. It seems to me that is something about which the government should concern itself in great measure.
There is another phase to this. It seems to me that because these bond prices were established at an artificially high level for the purpose of the bond conversion-an artificially high level bearing in mind the depressed condition of the bond market at that time-and because the issues I have mentioned were included, in the conversion operation although they had several years to run that the conversion was bound to be a failure notwithstanding the language of the Minister of Finance. When I say it was bound to be a failure, I mean not so much in the premise of the number of bonds converted-that is not the point I am seeking to make-but in the light of the objectives of the conversion loan. As I indicated a moment ago, during the conversion loan the Bank of Canada acquired a very large volume of victory bonds for cash. The reason for that I have indicated; it was simply because they fixed an artificially high value at that time.
In order to curb the consequent increase in the cash reserves of the chartered banks,
Monetary Policy
and because of the acquisition of these victory bonds, the Bank of Canada had to sell treasury bills and short term bonds on the market. I want to develop this thesis a little further. The Bank of Canada at the end of the period during which the conversion loan was offered converted large amounts of its victory bonds into new long term conversion issues. As a consequence the average term of its portfolio was largely changed by being very substantially lengthened. In a moment I want to take the actual figures.
I am glad to see the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Macdonnell) is interested in this matter. I think it is something he appreciates and follows most attentively, and I appreciate his interest in it. As a consequence of what I have described, the average term of the Bank of Canada's portfolio was substantially lengthened. I will give figures in a moment to prove this contention. This, it will be seen, materially reduced the capacity of the Bank of Canada to carry out open market operations in short term securities.
Let me point out to the hon. gentleman that as at December 31, 1958, the Bank of Canada held $1,326 million worth of bonds with a maturity date over ten years, which was some $1,113 million more than it held at the beginning of the year. This information will be found, if the minister wishes to check my figures, on page 91 of the Bank of Canada statistical summary for March, 1959. He will see there that at the end of December 1957 the bank's holdings of maturities of a term longer than ten years were $213.3 million but that at the end of December, 1958 the Bank of Canada's holdings of such maturities had increased to $1,326.4 million-an increase by more than six times in the course of a year. That is, the bank's holdings of bonds having maturity terms of more than ten years was multiplied more than six times in the period between the end of December 1957 and the end of December 1958.
In this connection I want to suggest one thing to the Minister of Finance. He spoke about the victory loan bonds overhanging the market. Let me suggest to him that it is these very large holdings of long term bonds by the Bank of Canada which are overhanging the market today. These long term bonds in the Bank of Canada's portfolio are a dead weight overhanging the market. They are, to a considerable extent, undermining confidence in the stability of long term bonds and in the level of bond yields. I think the minister will agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I disagree entirely as to the effect.

Monetary Policy
Well, the facts speak for themselves. If the minister wants to draw a different conclusion it is open to him to do so.
The minister is a prejudiced witness.

In any event, investors in Canada consider that they do constitute a dead weight hanging over the market today, and in their minds at least this is a matter of some consequence.
There is another consequence of this wholly unsuccessful conversion loan that I wish to draw to the attention of the house, namely the undue expansion of the money supply. It is clear from the Bank of Canada's report that in order to carry out the loan of May 1, the loan of $950 million, it was necessary to expand the money supply by a substantial amount. That is how I read the Bank of Canada report. This loan was a prelude to the conversion loan and both loans had the same characteristic; that is, that the money supply was expanded in order to facilitate each of them. During the period of the conversion loan the money supply, that is the total currency and chartered bank deposits, expanded from some $12,385 million to $13,098 million-an increase of some $713 million in two months.
The story of this increase in the money supply will be found in considerable detail at page 99 of the March statistical summary of the Bank of Canada. The figures are quite interesting. They certainly support the thesis I am advancing, and I think they are capable of no other interpretation than that these two bond issues brought about a direct and very sharp increase in the money supply, an increase which might be described, as unprecedented in peacetime.
Whatever the views of the Minister of Finance may be in this connection, the investors have shown a pronounced lack of confidence in the bond market. The hon. gentleman has claimed that his loan issues have had the effect of stabilizing the bond market. My view is that they have had the very opposite effect and that the minister's claim is totally unfounded. The effect of the conversion loan was to undermine confidence in the bond market.
There is another interesting facet of this subject. The Bank of Canada has been obliged to take active steps to support the market for the long term conversion loan. Such an operation could not be successfully carried out at a time when there is an underlying lack of confidence in the market without the bank acquiring, and ending up with, large holdings. That is exactly what took place

last fall, and during the fall months the money supply was further expanded by some $300 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Last fall?
Yes. 1 have the figures here and I can put them on record.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are wrong about that.

No, I am right. I can put the figures on record and perhaps, if the minister is in doubt about them, I should do so.
The total currency and chartered bank deposits, as indicated at page 99 of the March statistical summary issued by the Bank of Canada, is shown on December 31, 1957 as being $11,923 million, and the total at December 31, 1958, is shown as being $13,247 million. I used the term "last fall". If the minister will look at the figure for the end of September he will find it stood at some $13,022 million, and that at the end of October it was $13,347 million or an increase, in a 31-day period, of some $325 million. I do not know how there could be stronger evidence in support of my statement than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member said "the fall". The fact is that from the first of October there was no increase in the money supply at all.

Let me repeat the figures, Mr. Speaker, because I think the minister has not followed the details given in the statistical summary. At the end of September the figure for the total currency and chartered banks deposits stood at some $13,022 million. At the end of October the figure was some $13,347 million. That is an increase of $325 million in the 31 days of October alone. I do not know what could be more pronounced than that. What the minister has apparently lost sight of is the fact that later on in the year the money supply remained comparatively constant. If he will bring his figure up to the last date I have here, March 25, he will find that it is some $13,219 million. This shows that to support the conversion issue itself the government in effect had to increase the money supply. I think the minister will agree with this conclusion which may be drawn from the figures I have just quoted.
Apparently confronted with the dilemma of having to continue to support this long term conversion issue the bank withdrew its support and let the conversion issue find its own level. Let me point out that when it got itself into the position I have described the bank, considering the obligations imposed on it by the law, withdrew its support. How those bonds went down. It was a pretty cruel

blow to the individual bondholders who had accepted at their face value the very stirring and rousing appeals made by the government for them to convert to those issues. Their reward was a reduction in price in some cases to as low as $92.50.
I always understood that one of the prime objectives of this loan was to clear the decks to enable the government to finance its cash deficit of some $1.4 billion of additional money which it required to raise. I think that is a fair statement. The government would have liked to finance that additional new borrowing by selling bonds to the general public and to avoid sharp and abnormal increases in the money supply. I believe that is a fair statement of the objectives. However, as I have indicated, in order to dispose of the May 1 issue and make the conversion loan appear to be a success according to the way the Minister of Finance viewed it, the government did the very thing it tried to avoid. It expanded the money supply to the extent of some $1,467 million between the end of March and the end of October; that is in the period it was financing the bond issue of May 1 and the conversion loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that the government expanded the money supply?

Technically it was done
through the Bank of Canada. That was the effect of this policy. The government produced this situation by its wholly wrong concept of what should be done with respect to the conversion loan. I say that is certainly a direct consequence of the government's action in following the course it did in the circumstances existing at that time. This matter of financing bonds by creating a new money supply is a dangerous proposition. In my view this situation was brought about largely by the government's own action, its whole monetary policy, its sins of omission and commission, its public policies, as well as its mishandling of the national accounts. The point I want to make clear is that the conversion loan resulted in this expanded money supply and did the very thing it was supposed to avoid. In other words it failed in its major objectives.
Another thing it did in addition to what I have mentioned is that it failed completely to restore the confidence of the investing public. For instance, in October and December the government offered new bond issues. If the minister will check the figures he will find that those operations resulted in a loss to the bond buyers. I think he will agree that prices have gone down on those issues.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But that does not mean a loss.
Monetary Policy
It is certainly not a gain.

Of major significance is the fact that it is not the kind of thing that creates confidence in the investing public. It tends to make the investing public lose confidence in this government's method of handling monetary policies and in this bond issue. That atmosphere of disillusionment among the people who would normally invest in bonds is a very serious thing. It spread generally among individual bond buyers, corporation treasurers, insurance companies, the holders of bonds generally; and in my judgment based on reading their accounts it spread through the commercial banks all across the country. As I have said, it was due to a considerable degree to the raising of hopes by government spokesmen and the subsequent dashing of those hopes after the bonds had been purchased.
Let me illustrate my point. I believe the government itself has been somewhat infected by the loss of confidence in what it is doing. We observe that the government has done some unusual things in bond financing. Allow me to deal with one of them. I am seeking to illustrate the uncertainty of the government's policy in the monetary field. Let me take the bond issue maturing April 1, 1960. It was a 23 per cent issue, issued at $97.90 and the effective yield, I believe, was 4.76 per cent. It was issued for a term of thirteen months. Permit me to point out a little side repercussion of that bond issue which also tended to undermine confidence in the government's policy in this field.
The effective yield may be stated to be 4.76 per cent, but the effective yield to an investor who is in the 50 per cent income tax bracket is something quite different again. The yield provided by that bond is exactly the same as if such an investor bought at par a bond bearing an interest coupon of 6.6 per cent per annum. If anyone doubts how that works out I could place it on the record, but I believe it is quite clear. If you take the portion of the increase in capital within the thirteen months-that is 12/13 of that figure-and take that portion of the net gain of the purchaser together with the interest which he has at the end of the year, after taking his 50 per cent income tax off, you will find he is in the same circumstances as if he had bought a bond at par but having a yield of 6.6 per cent. In my opinion that is something that the government should not be proud of. It is not the kind of thing that creates confidence in investors although to a few investors it is a very fortunate circumstance.

Monetary Policy

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Liberal government did it many times.

The Liberal government did not do it many times. I want to clear up that canard once and for all. I expected that interjection. If the minister will check the records he will find that when the Liberal government issued bonds below their face value, as indeed it did on many occasions, the bonds were of long term, the interest rate was lower and there was no such windfall to be made out of them. There were no 13-month or other short term bonds of that sort issued in that way by the Liberal government. I am glad the minister interjected because it gives me the opportunity to answer that canard once and for all.
There is another side to the operation of this particular issue of bonds. The minister does not explain that by that method the tax collecting authority, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), receives a little less in tax collections than he would if interest were payable on the whole gain of the persons who bought the bonds. Therefore, in effect the tax load is distributed over those persons who did not buy the bonds because they are in the smaller income tax brackets. Surely the minister is not very proud or happy about that.
As I have said, the general public have been losing confidence in the government's ability in this field. They have lost all confidence in the worth of the bonds under present government management. That seems to me to be a very serious thing. These people were promised a good thing in buying these bonds. They were subjected to an abnormally intensive selling program. Perhaps it could be more appropriately described as ballyhoo but in any event there was a very strong, intensive selling program. The people were told that it was in the national interest to convert and that it would fight inflation. Surely in all this there was some implication that the bonds would maintain their value.
But we find now that the measures used in this whole transaction not only did not fight inflation but were directly inflationary. The fear of inflation has not subsided. The national interest in this respect has not been served by the conversion loan. Rather, the national interest has been dealt a cruel blow by this aspect of the conversion loan.
I indicated that we have had a very substantial increase in the money supply. In addition, I want to point out that for all practical purposes new borrowings in the year 1958 amounted to $1,360 million. As set out on page 7 of the Bank of Canada report, that amount is made up of some $1,250 million in new direct and guaranteed securities and

to be added to that is the figure of $110 million representing the reduction in the holdings in government accounts. The minister can argue whether the correct figure should be $1,250 million or $1,360 million; it is open to argument but the explanation is to be found on page 7 of the Bank of Canada report. In any event, it is a very large figure.
But during the same period of time when the increase in borrowings was taking place the money supply increased by $1,324 million, from $11,923 million at December 31, 1957 to $13,247 million at December 31, 1958. The increase of $1,324 million in the money supply is very close to the amount of new government borrowings. In fact, it is almost identical. In the light of that fact, I confess I was completely unable to understand the argument of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his budget speech this year when he tended to indicate that government borrowings over the year as a whole had been achieved largely in a non-inflationary manner. So that the minister will understand my reasoning I refer him to his own budget speech, page 2415 of Hansard, where he will find he made that statement. I do not know anything that could be more inflationary than an increase in the money supply of that magnitude at that time, an increase in the money supply almost identical with the total borrowings of the government in the same period.
The government has produced another economic paradox by its monetary operations. At the same time as the sharp increase in the money supply, which many would term as easy money, we have had a sharp and very large increase in the interest rate. In popular terms we have what may be called easy money and dear money both at the same time. We have today the highest bank rate in the country's history with all its implications, all its ramifications with respect to government borrowings in the future, the high interest charges that will have to be paid on such borrowings and the effect it will have on provincial and municipal borrowings and borrowings by the private sector of the economy.
My goodness, when the members of the present government were in opposition I used to hear them argue about the evils and consequences of high interest rates. I often wonder what they think about that matter now. I will not embarrass them today with all their arguments on the subject but they are many. Indeed, if they believed those arguments they must be having a very unpleasant time now.

But we have this paradox. The last treasury bill rate announced was 4.72 per cent, an alltime high. I want to point out that the rate is very high compared with the United States rate. I want to emphasize the widening of the gap between the Canadian and the United States rates. I also wish to suggest to the minister that if he chooses to answer he might deal with the extent to which the widening gap is due to a loss of confidence by the Canadian people in the government of our country. I should also like him to contemplate the adverse effects on our economy that the widening gap, in addition to the high rate, may have. Incidentally, the last rate I have for United States treasury bills is 3.10 per cent compared with 4.72 per cent in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the date?

I have it noted on my copy of the last weekly supplement. I will give you the date in a moment; I have it here. I have not got it in my hand, but I think I can find it later. It was 3.07 per cent the previous date, but I think it has gone up from 3.07 per cent to 3.10 per cent.
I want now to take the minister back to the argument which he advanced in referring to the conversion loan as the foundation for a sound debt management operation. If indeed it was such a foundation, then I want to point out that that foundation has failed miserably. It has contributed to an increase in the money supply to unprecedented high levels and to increasing the interest rate to an unprecedented high level. It is really a foundation to inflation, pure and simple.
The minister talked about reduced federal borrowings to leave room for existing dominion-provincial financing. I can only point out to him that if that is what he is planning to do by his monetary policies, then by his own actions he has left to the provinces and municipalities the right to borrow at extremely high interest rates. They are simply not in a position to do so.
I take the minister's position to be, as he has indicated, that he believes that the rate of personal savings in 1959 will be lower and as we proceed on the road to recovery the business sector will require more funds. If business conditions improve, and I for one certainly hope they do, it is reasonable to expect some liquidation of holdings of bonds by corporations and banks.
In addition to that, the government itself has to face the current requirements of 195960. Perhaps before I deal with these current requirements I should point out to the minister another instance of what has taken place under his policy, and that is the virtual removal from the Bank of Canada portfolio of 66968-9-195
Monetary Policy
short term treasury bill holdings. If he will look at page 91 of the March statistical summary he will find that during the time when there was a very sharp increase taking place in long term holdings, that is holdings of bonds having maturity of over 10 years, there was a correspondingly sharp reduction in the holdings of treasury bills. This summary indicates that from the end of March, which was just prior to the first borrowings of last year, the Bank of Canada's holding of treasury bills dropped from some $480 million, and dropped almost continuously and regularly, to a low of $6 million at the end of January, 1959. Since then, they have only increased slightly to $161 million at the end of March.
He will find also that their holdings of short term bonds, that is two years and under, have dropped from some $1,009 million at the end of April to some $91 million at the end of March of this year. There has been a similar but smaller drop in the holdings of bonds with maturities from two to five years. In other words, the bank has switched its portfolio to these long term bonds, so that they overhang the market. The bank has taken away from itself the ability to meet its requirements easily to support certain short term issues. The minister will see the seriousness of that dilemma. Incidentally, if he doubts what I have said about the loss of confidence in government bonds, if he will take the corresponding table which I do not propose to put on the record, for holdings by private individuals, he will see that of the total increase of bonds in the hands of the public almost exactly 50 per cent is in Canada savings bonds and short term treasury bills. The public have put themselves in a position where they can deal with short term securities and liquidate them as they see fit.
I was speaking of the requirements for the current year, and in speaking about that I think I must rely on the figures-I hope the minister will just catch these figures before he goes out-given by the minister in his budget speech, when he said that following the replacement of the cash deficit he will possibly have a budgetary and capital deficit of some $850 million. In addition to that, there are the bond maturities for this year, and if we include the maturities of April 1, 1960 the day after the end of the fiscal year the total will be $1,735 million. In other words, the country is confronted with finding this year by way of replacement of existing maturities and for new purposes, additional sums to the amount of $2,585 million, a very large sum indeed.
Well, you may ask how did we get ourselves into this horrible condition? I suggest that same question has been asked in other

Monetary Policy
places but has not been answered here. For instance, we find that the United States was concerned about some of these problems as far back as a year ago. We find that on August 18, 1958, Mr. Henry Hazlitt, as reported in Newsweek, in talking about inflation had this to say:
It is time to ask some blunt questions of congress and the administration. Do you ever expect the debt to be paid oil? Do you ever intend even to reduce it? If so, at what rate? Under what conditions? Are the conditions likely to be realized? Do you intend to pay off either principal or interest in dollars of even present (48 cent) purchasing power, or do you mean to keep short-changing the government's creditors by further depreciation?
Mr. Speaker, in that jurisdiction the President of the United States did indicate that he is seeking to balance the budget; he did indicate other policies that would seek to deal with the problem. In Canada there are also others concerned with this problem. On Saturday I received the eighty-ninth annual report of the Mutual Life Assurance Company of Canada. I find that in dealing with economic matters generally the president had something to say in his report which in my judgment is equally applicable to the problem we are discussing today, namely the minister's actions in the field of monetary policy. I would like to place the quotation on Hansard. The president had this to say:
What can be done toward building a sound national economic policy?
Then, he answered his own question in this way:
First, aim at improving the psychological atmosphere by making clear that every effort will be made to return sound dollars for the money our governments are now borrowing. This calls for action, not merely exhortation. It is a matter of honesty as well as economic good sense. A heavy responsibility rests on the federal government in this regard, for it is the only debtor which can exercise direct influence over the value of the currency in which its obligations will be repaid.
Mr. Speaker, the government has got itself into this position mainly through its own actions. To meet the problem that confronts us by way of borrowing the minister has told us that he expects the Canada savings bonds will yield about $250 million; but the big question outstanding is as to the policy to be applied in providing for the rest of the requirements. I will admit that the minister is facing a real dilemma. He can either increase the money supply or he can, I suppose, offer still higher interest rates for new government bonds. Let me point out it is quite clear that the governor of the Bank of Canada is opposed to an increase in the money supply at this stage. If we look at page 9 of the annual report we will find this statement:
The central bank must continue to emphasize its major and essential role of regulating the rate of
[Mr. Mcllraith.l
change in overall monetary supplies in such manner as is consistent with and, so far as monetary action can, will contribute to, sound and sustained economic growth under stable prices.
I believe that monetary policy must strengthen and reaffirm its determination to remain true to the basic principles of sound money.
Certainly that is not what was done last year. It is certain that any material increase in the money supply will produce greater inflation and rising prices. I can only hope that the Minister of Finance will agree with the reasoning of the governor of the Bank of Canada and that the bond issue will not be created out of an increased money supply.
The other method, of course, is providing money by borrowing by paying a further increase in bond yield and that, I think, is going to be pretty unacceptable to the taxpayers and pretty unacceptable to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Are you in favour of it?

I am in complete accord with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) that I am not always authorized to speak for the government, and certainly not for this present government.
Higher interest rates have as a necessary corollary to other borrowings that they would discourage private investors, that is private investors who would be borrowers, and they would also put the provinces and municipalities in a wholly intolerable position. This is the dilemma the government is in, largely through its own doing.
There is another method, I suppose, which could be used in dealing with this problem, and it has to do with the demands for money credit allocation. Quite a bit is said about this in the Bank of Canada report at page 7 and onward and I should like to quote some of it:
If recovery and growth proceed very strongly the demand for money to finance apparently desirable projects-both the desirability and the number of which multiply rapidly under such circumstances- may once again increase more rapidly than the supply of savings and of loanable funds. Under such conditions also the demand for capital and credit for speculative or non-productive purposes would increase and become a strong competitor for money.
I think there can be nothing but agreement with this statement. Then the report goes on, on the next page, to point out that if such scarcity of funds develops it is the government's responsibility and not the bank's to take whatever measures that are taken designed to alleviate the credit squeeze which could victimize any segment of the borrowers or any certain group of borrowers. His exact words can be found on page 9 of the report,

and I have no desire to quote them other than the very last sentence where he says:
Regardless of the desirability or feasibility of these measures, they are outside the powers of the Bank of Canada.
There is, of course, always another method that could be used and it is interesting to note that Mr. Fraser Robertson, in writing on this subject in the Globe and Mail of April 16, had this to say:
Bluntly, that means that if the government cannot get money, or have money provided for what it considers necessary purposes, on a voluntary basis, it will use coercion.
There is a fourth method, of course, namely that of coercion. I think the implications of such government control over the capital market are not something that we, or anyone in the house, contemplate without the greatest concern, and I would hope that all would agree that this method is to be avoided. Yet the government has created a situation by its own actions which invites questions like these to be raised. It has not outlined to parliament its plans for dealing with our financial difficulties.
Surely, the government, having created the highest deficit in our peacetime history, with the announced intention of having the second highest deficit in the current fiscal year, and with nothing to indicate other than recurring deficits; having created the highest debt charges in the history of Canada; having increased the money supply by the greatest amount in any peacetime year and created doubt in the investing public's minds by these inflationary methods of doing its financing in the last fiscal year; having created the highest interest rates for years and years; having done all these things through its policies owes it to the country and to this house to outline its program and policy in the field of debt management, and its monetary policies.
These difficulties in which we find ourselves in this respect today are, as I have sought to indicate, largely of the government's doings. They have been substantially contributed to by them. I believe that the government is subject to censure for its ill-conceived and irresponsible actions in this field.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget), that:
All the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor :
"this house regrets the ill-conceived and irresponsible actions of the government in the field of deDt management and monetary policy which have been characterized by:
1.	The errors and inequities associated with the conversion loan:
66968-9-195J
Monetary Policy
2.	The highest bank rate since the Bank of Canada was established:
3.	The largest expansion of the money supply in any year since the war;
4.	The greatest increase in peacetime in the national debt;
5.	The highest public debt charges in Canada's history."

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to a point of order, if I may, before the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) rises. It is in submission quite clear that the amendment which has just been submitted by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) repeats in large measure the amendment which was introduced in this house on April 13 by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) on the budget. I do not say it repeats it in full but it repeats a good deal of it. Because it repeats a good deal of it, I submit it is clearly out of order. May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, of the language of the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River on April 13, which is to be found in Hansard at page 2619, the second column:
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house regrets the bad faith of the government, which sought and secured support from the Canadian people on a program of lower taxes, reduced expenditures and a balanced budget, and which has now produced, in flagrant disregard of pre-election promises, a budget calling for higher taxes, record expenditures and a large deficit."
Mr. Speaker, we have noted, of course, that in his remarks leading up to his amendment the hon. member for Ottawa West has simply threshed straw which was threshed for eight days in this chamber in the course of the budget debate. These matters were touched on from time to time in discussion.
Touched on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Examine, if you will, the language of this amendment. It touches on the conversion loan, the Bank of Canada rate, the expansion of money supply, the increase in the national debt, and then the highest public debt charges in Canada's history. These are all matters associated, Mr. Speaker, with the subject of the attempted indictment in the amendment of April 13: the higher taxes, the record expenditures and the large deficit. Surely, Mr. Speaker, however much effort has been expended to try to devise today an amendment which will somehow steer clear of repetition of any part of the amendment of April 13, the draftsman of this amendment has not succeeded.
For an amendment to be out of order on this occasion, Mr. Speaker, it is not necessary, in the light of former decisions, that it should cover entirely the language and purport of

Monetary Policy
the amendment of April 13. It is sufficient if it covers part of the area covered by the amendment of April 13. This amendment certainly does, Mr. Speaker. One cannot discuss any of these matters without trespassing again upon the realm of the budget debate and the language, as well as the purport, of the amendment of April 13. Mr. Speaker, in the light of the fact that at least part of the area covered by the amendment of April 13 is covered by today's amendment and that amendment of April 13 was rejected by the house by vote last week, in my respectful submission the present amendment is out of order and I ask it be so ruled.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might be permitted to say a word or two on the point of order raised by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming): I should like to point out that if we look at the terms of the amendment proposed by the member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) and then compare it with the amendment proposed by the member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), as found on page 2619 of Hansard for April 13, it is my humble submission that each of the five complaints of the member for Ottawa West could obtain even if you had lower taxes, lower expenditures and a balanced budget. There might be some question as to No. 4, the greatest increase in peacetime in the national debt. However, may I point out that you could have a balanced budget and at the same time have heavy government borrowings on behalf of crown corporations. Such borrowings do not come into the picture as far as a balanced budget is concerned. So each of the five complaints in the amendment of the Liberal party could obtain even with lower taxes, lower expenditures and a balanced budget. Therefore it is our contention that the amendment is not out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw to your attention one matter which seems to have been missed in the argument. The budget has to do with the national accounts and their administration by the government. It is a motion to go into committee of ways and means and is the traditional period in which the minister accounts for the receipts and disbursements of the government. The amendment today has nothing to do with that subject at all and is not couched in language capable of giving it that interpretation. Mr. Speaker, I would draw your attention to the fact that if the argument of the Minister of Finance were to be accepted no further subject matter of any kind could be brought before the house, because in some way or another the subject would have some relationship to something in the budget. It

would be utterly impossible to bring any motion before the house for that reason.
However, I would like to draw your attention to the proposed amendment itself. The amendment is concerned with the ill-conceived and irresponsible actions of the government in the field of debt management and monetary policy. Surely it cannot be held that that is the same thing as lower taxes, reduced expenditures and a balanced budget, all of which were talked about in the amendment moved in the course of the budget debate. It is a wholly different subject, Mr. Speaker.
It is true that the mismanagement we allege in debt financing could indirectly affect the budget, but it is a wholly different subject matter. The amendment is one dealing with the field of debt management and monetary policy. Then the amendment gives a list by way of illustration of some of the incidents of mismanagement in that field.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I add a word on the point of order? The main portion of this amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) is:
This house regrets the ill-conceived and irresponsible actions of the government in the field of debt management and monetary policy which have been characterized by-
And then it goes on to list five so-called examples. But the essence of the amendment is contained in the first three lines. Surely that is an amendment to the budget. The purpose of the budget debate is to discuss these very things and, particularly, monetary policy. That is the essence of a budget debate, and in the attack which was made during the budget debate by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) he took in effect exactly the same position as that which the hon. member for Ottawa West is taking today. In fact there has been a great deal of repetition in the speech which the hon. member for Ottawa West made this afternoon of what was said during the budget debate. If an amendment of this type, which is really a budgetary amendment, can be moved now, I would suggest that a similar amendment could be moved on the next supply motion simply by using words other than "debt management" and "monetary policy". Surely that was never the intention. The rules of the house provide for one budget debate which is supposed to deal with monetary policy. That debate has been held, and it finished only last week. Now we have another amendment put forward by the opposition which, in effect, I suggest is nothing more or less than a budget amendment and which, as such, is out of order.

I should like to make a few observations based on those which have just been made by the leader of the house. The motion which is made by the minister of finance when he introduces the budget is, as Your Honour knows, that Your Honour should leave the chair. To say that anything said during the budget debate is decided by the house is, of course, not in accordance with the established rules. The amendments to the budget are therefore all that can be considered as limiting the freedom to go into supply, that is, amendments to the budget and any other matters which have already been settled by the house, and it seems to me that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) and the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) have sufficiently disposed of the argument made by the Minister of Finance that there is any conflict between this motion and the motion moved by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. The minister did, of course, refer only to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, there was also the amendment to the amendment.

There was the amendment to the amendment, but there was no conflict there, it seems to me, either. But if Your Honour is satisfied there is no need for further argument I will be very glad to sit down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I had rather thought, in view of the discussion which took place in the house on Friday, that the house had itself come to the conclusion that a discussion on the problem of interest rates could be expected today, and that caused me some difficulty, because there was a fairly specific subamendment about interest rates which was moved in the course of the budget debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: April 13.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes. And then again, this present amendment does not take that course. There is no mention of interest rates in the amendment as submitted. Therefore, I suppose that that approach to the subject.

that this was a debate which the house was expecting-really does not apply.
The point of order that we are entering upon a repetition of matters which have been decided must, I think, be judged in the light of what the procedure is on supply motions. Supply motions give a great deal of latitude for attack on the policy of the government on a fairly broad front, and I think that almost any supply motion would involve monetary and financial problems in some degree. But I am not satisfied from what
Monetary Policy
the hon. minister has said that this amendment cannot be distinguished from the debate which took place on the budget. The budget deals with ways and means. It deals with taxation and expenditures, and the balance of the two. In other words, it is basically a taxation debate. This motion, to my mind, introduces the problem of public debt and public debt management, and it does not seem to me that the two fields entirely corresponds. They overlap, it is true, but they are not co-equal, in the sense that the policy of the government with regard to the conversion loan is carried out entirely outside the budget resolutions and reflects independent actions of the government under authority which parliament has previously given.
As I look at the resolution it seems to refer to debt management and monetary policy basically, and the five instances cited have to do with the conversion loan, the public debt, the bank rate, which is not directly involved in the budget-I see I am in error in saying that interest is not involved, because the bank rate is a matter of interest-the expansion of money supply-something which could be independent of the budget debate and budget resolutions-the national debt itself, and public debt charges.
I would think there is scope for a debate on public debt management as distinct from the other fiscal policies which are involved in the budget. In any event, I would be disposed to consider the amendment liberally in view, first of all, of the fact that this is a supply motion and, second, in view of what was said in this house on Friday. In that light I would hope that the opposition to this resolution would not be pressed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to two points, first to the amendment to the amendment which was moved in the budget debate on April 13 and which also covered part of the ground that is sought to be covered in the amendment now submitted. That subamendment reads, as recorded in Hansard at page 2623:
That . . . this house further regrets that the government has failed to present to parliament a planned financial and economic program designed to develop the economic health of the nation by, among other things, (a) reversing the trend of rising interest rates-
That question is presented again today.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, we have
presented to us an attempt at an indictment based upon the highest bank rate since the Bank of Canada was established, Vhich is

Monetary Policy
part and parcel of the same complaint which was made in the C.C.F. subamendment moved in the budget debate.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As to what happened last Friday, may I point out that while some things were said about a discussion today, the Prime Minister, as reported at page 3013, was very careful to point out that the rules must, of course, apply with regard to any motion that might be introduced. Here are his words as reported in Hansard in the first column of that page. After the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) had attributed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) what he called a suggestion that we should have a supply motion on Monday on the particular kind of amendment now under discussion, that is, an amendment relating to interest, the Prime Minister replied:
No, not at all. There was no such suggestion. I said that opportunity would come on Monday, taut as far as the rules are concerned the question still remains as to the propriety or regularity of such a motion.
There cannot be any suggestion that so far as this present amendment is concerned there was any agreement on the part of the Prime Minister or anyone else in this house to waive the rules of this house in regard to what is propriety and order on an amendment of this kind.
With great respect it is my submission, Mr. Speaker, that the ground in regard to the issue as to rising interest rates has already been covered by these two previous amendments which have been disposed of by vote of the house.
The final point I should like to mention is as to whether this present matter of debt management was embraced within the scope of the budget. With great respect I submit that was very much a part of the budget presentation. There will be found at page 2411 of the budget speech as recorded in Hansard a section extending over two and a half pages devoted to that very subject. The heading there is "Debt Management". That subject certainly was discussed in the course of the budget debate. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) also had something to say about it. This, it seems to me, disposes of any suggestion that we are here today breaking new ground and that the amendment now submitted breaks new ground that was not included within the scope of both the amendment and the amendment to the amendment during the budget debate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am inclined to accept the latter argument of the minister that anything to be said on this amendment could have

been said on the budget debate but that does not say this amendment is out of order; it points up certain and particular problems.
As I recall the budget debate the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) was the only hon. member who spoke for any length on the conversion loan and he was in order in speaking there, but this amendment focuses the attention of the house on monetary policy in the sense of the national debt and its management as well as certain other things of a specific character.
I have doubts about the second item in the amendment which refers to the highest bank rate. As I said, I expected that was the course this amendment would take and I realize that anything said on Friday, unless there is an order of the house, does not absolve me from the responsibility of dealing with this amendment on its merits today. I should think the house would understand from what I have said that I am disposed to regard this as a suitable amendment and to let it proceed reserving the right to limit the discussion under the second item of the amendment, because, as the minister has pointed out, we have had a specific amendment accusing the government of failure to act against high interest rates which is what is involved, I take it, in the clause "highest bank rates since the Bank of Canada was established". It may be possible to distinguish those. I would allow the debate to proceed and reserve the right to intervene if I feel that it is becoming a repetition of the budget debate.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) and particularly to those comments referring to the one facet of our fiscal problems that concerns us at the present time. I would say that in general this group can support this amendment but I want to make some qualifications with respect to clause 3 of the amendment which reads as follows:
-the largest expansion of the money supply in any year since the war.
Under our present unplanned economy unrelated to monetary and fiscal policies, that is an evil. In the opinion of this group the expansion of the money supply would be quite a safe proposal if it were related to a planned economic policy and the planned development of this country. With that qualification we in this group can support this amendment.
I was somewhat interested in the failure of the hon. member for Ottawa West to make any alternative proposals with respect to his criticism of the government's fiscal policy.

I am one who is rather inclined to symbolize ideas, groups and things of that sort. While he was speaking I could not help thinking that all three parties in this house could be well represented or symbolized by certain animals. I would say the Progressive Conservatives would be well represented by the porcupine. As we know, they are inclined to climb a tree, look down on the rest of the world and shed their quills when annoyed, as the minister does on occasion. I would say the Liberals would be well represented by the rabbit. They are quite harmless, quite neutral and not given to construction or things of that sort. They are nice as a pet, particularly for children and people with immature minds. So far as our group is concerned it is obvious that there is only one animal by which it could be represented and that is the beaver. It is always building.
As I look over at the Minister of Finance I have memories of him when he was in opposition. At that time I used to regard him as a sort of symbolized connoisseur of the evils of waste and extravagance, high interest rates, high taxes and consequent inflation. I used to think of him as the lion rampant of the opposition roaring his demands for the remedy of these evils. According to the records, the last time I heard him roar in this respect was in the budget debate on March 21, 1957. Anyone taking the time to go back and read that debate will be most interested in observing how the minister has changed his tune. He is singing quite a different tune today, now that he has assumed the responsibility of the portfolio of Minister of Finance.
When I witness his present mellow meekness which represents such a marked change, his pallid smile in the face of opposition criticism, it appears to me that the former lion rampant of the opposition has become the minister quiescent. The minister has our sympathy and what we shall do this afternoon is to present constructive alternatives designed to bail the minister out of his very difficult situation. I want him to understand that our policy and program will be presented with the best intentions and in the best spirit.
It may be asked why the minister has our sympathy. He has it because he is the victim of circumstances, caught in the vise of the inherent contradictions of capitalism -I am now speaking as a democractic socialist-and also in the contradictions of the speeches he made while in opposition and those he has made as Minister of Finance. He is caught also by his party's philosophy, election problems and present policies which policies permitted the gain of $165 million by certain people who benefited by the conversion loan and also the looting of the
Monetary Policy
public wealth of this country by certain persons who buy stock and make no contribution to the wealth of Canada at the same time. The minister is also caught in the vise of fixed interest charges, statutory payments and also the present recession and unemployment problems for which this government is not entirely without responsibility.
In the opinion of this group all this results from a system which leaves genuine economic control in the hands of a few people without direct responsibility to all the people in this country. Proof of this I think is clearly provided in the recent price increases, exceeding the tax increases, on the part of certain people who have things to sell in Canada whose actions in this regard were deplored even by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). I wonder what some of the same people would say if all wage earners in this country demanded an automatic increase in wages equal to the increase in taxes and the increase in the cost of living occasioned by the increase in prices by these people who accept no social responsibility to the country as a whole.
There is no question but that unemployment and inflation are the two current, major national problems. As a result of this amendment I intend to deal with the problem of inflation which is more correctly termed a debasement of currency. Whom does it affect? It is a very serious problem at this time which I think is being underestimated in some quarters. It affects all the working people of the country and the real value of their wages. It has affected farm costs and prices and we realized from the representations made by the delegation which came from the prairie provinces recently. It has affected our small business people. It has affected our young people trying to obtain an education. A good many young Canadians were unable to return to universities last fall because they could not obtain employment last summer. It has certainly affected the standard of living of our senior citizens. I am sure all members of the house have had representations in that connection.
To illustrate that point I want to read very briefly from an article in the Ottawa Citizen of Thursday, August 16 entitled "Welfare Report; 273,000 Ontario Aged In Impoverished State". It reads in part as follows:
Between 180,000 and 273,000 of Ontario residents over 60 are living below a subsistence level, it was estimated yesterday.
This is largely occasioned at the present time by the increases in the cost of living and the low standard of their allowances. I think we should all recognize the fact that persons of small means, small earning power,

Monetary Policy
small income are always much more seriously affected by inflation or debasement of currency than persons of larger means or big business. Why? Because big business, industrialists or manufacturers, almost always have their entire wealth invested in natural resources or in equity capital which gives them ownership and control of the plants in question. That is why tremendous inflation oc-cured in Germany after the first world war. The Krupps and others, the warmongers generally, suffered nothing. Their interest was in equity shares in their plants. The working people of that country suffered tremendously, and that was one reason why Hitler obtained their support at a later time.
Inflation or debasement of currency is caused by irresponsible, unplanned development, a lack of direction and tempo of investment, government fiscal policy, monopoly regulated prices, which has actually happened at the present time as I will demonstrate later, and lack of markets. Before proceeding with concrete proposals, as a democratic socialist I do wish to mention a few axioms with respect to inflation which we consider is an eruption of capitalism, a periodic disease because of the lack of control by governments of the economic system of the country which they are supposed to govern. I think we should not forget these axioms.
The first, in my opinion, is that value is determined by the amount of necessary labour incorporated in the production of the required amount of a commodity. Second, the production of any commodity over the required quantity does not add any value by way of the excess. For instance, the production of
1,000	tons of potatoes if the market requires only 500 tons will realize only the value of 500 tons. Inflation is not caused by high prices or high wages. Monopolies may vary the price to a limited degree. High monopoly prices tend to reduce the turnover and turnover is one of the most important objects of monopoly. If a commodity is sold above its value, money changes hands at less than its value. The commodity owner, if selling above value, takes a larger share of surplus value at the expense of the buyer capitalist. Sellers of labour power have excess included in their wages, as they have taxes. The eruption in capitalism, known as high prices or inflation, is the immediate effect of debasement of currency.
When we are dealing with this very complicated and difficult question I think we should remember some of these fundamental axioms. We do not suggest for a moment that this problem is an easy one which can be solved over night. We do maintain that, given correct policies, we can gradually work toward a solution of the problem. There 
are two major schools of thought when it comes to the question of inflation or the present situation which has developed through inflation. The classical school of thought-

Then I intend to put forward specific proposals. As a matter of fact, it is very hard to deal with monetary problems and policy without covering some previous ground that is related. I was saying that the classical economist sees the remedy to the situation in the arrested development of the economy, the restriction of the growth of social welfare services, a measure of unemployment and high interest rates. That is the classical approach to the situation we are experiencing at the present time.
What is the approach of democratic socialists? While we are conscious of the effect of inflation and the difficulties surrounding the problem, we believe it can be remedied by planned fiscal and economic policies and the planned direction and tempo of investment, which we think is very necessary. There is serious concern with this problem by a wide section of the community. I am sure all members realize that from their correspondence since the session commenced. Such correspondence largely relates, of course, to the increase in the cost of living. In that connection I want to quote from a few articles in various newspapers relating to this subject. I should like to read just the first paragraph from an interesting article in the Manchester Guardian of Saturday, February 14, 1959. It indicates the attitude of other countries toward the circumstances existing in Canada at this time. This is what the article has to say in part:
Canada has been since the war one of the most rapidly developing free countries in the world, and her natural resources make her future economic potential almost boundless. But she is approaching a dangerous cross-roads. Too few of her leaders seem to appreciate, or to be willing to give public warning of, her growing monetary and financial problems.

That is from a very substantial newspaper. I want to quote a comment on an article in Saturday Night entitled, "How the Banks Can Halt Inflation." I think it is a very good illustration of how government policy has permitted the banks to benefit from the present situation. It reads as follows:
An enlightening article on "How the Banks Can Halt Inflation" appeared in the February issue of Saturday Night. It was from the pen of Kenneth Gouldie. He relates how, prior to 1954, chartered banks were permitted by law to lend $10 in credit for every dollar held by the bank. That was the legal minimum cash reserve ratio. He goes on to tell how the Bank Act was amended in 1954 providing that the minimum reserve ratio be reduced from 10 per cent to 8 per cent. The writer then goes on to tell us exactly what happened as a result of this change and incidentally lets some light in on the way bankers become rich.
The Saturday Night article says: "During the first half of 1954 the mean cash reserve of the chartered banks amounted to a total of $894 million and the average amount of deposits (every loan being in fact a deposit) was $8,940 million. But in July of that year, after the legal minimum cash reserve ratio had been reduced to 8 per cent the banks could legally lend $11,170 million."
But that was not all that happened by reducing the reserve. Here is how Saturday Night tells it: "By consenting to reduction of the cash reserve ratio from 10 to 8 per cent, parliament then, in effect, made a gift worth $223 million to the shareholders of the chartered banks for which, in the higher prices of everything which Canadians have since bought and now buy, they have paid and are still paying."
I cannot blame the present government tor that action. Now that shows that government policy has an effect on the cost of living. There have been some other articles with respect to other persons who have an effect on the cost of living. I want to quote briefly from an article from the Ottawa Citizen of March 24, 1959 entitled "Price Increases and Inflation". It is quite brief. At one point, this article reads:
But one of the questions now being raised most consistently in hearings here is that the big steel and auto industries themselves may be equally to blame for unnecessary prices rises, which have helped the inflationary spiral. This view may have some application in Canada, too .. .
The more conservative economists have been unwilling to assess any blame to industry, but even some of them have admitted that the concentrated heavy industries, by their use of "administered prices", have contributed to the unique situation of the past two years, inflation in the midst of a severe recession. The theory of "administered prices" is that the few dominant corporations in the industry itself have the major control over pricing, rather than the market-place control by supply and demand.
And one noted economist, Gardner C. Means, who with Adolf A, Berle wrote a revolutionary volume on big business in the 1930's, "The Modern Corporation and Private Property", has been testifying to an increasingly interested group of senators that this is an entirely new type of inflation-an administered price inflation.
The heart of the Means thesis, which he buttresses with all kinds of charts and statistics, is that when 66968-9-196

big price increases come in the concentrated heavy industries like steel, rather than in the more competitive durable goods industries, it is largely because of administered pricing, and the effect of this rolls through all sections of the economy.
