I am coming right now to money supply; I am closer to it than I have ever been in my life before. I do want to emphasize that this indicates there is a possibility of regulated prices by large industries, such as steel, and I think we have to consider that in considering our proposals.
I want to mention a brief that was presented to the government on behalf of the united steelworkers of America concerning steel prices in Canada. On page 2 they suggest the government should require steel producers to make public the actual prices and price changes for all of their products.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry, but the hon. member does not seem to be paying very much attention to what I have said. He is going on to discuss the question of prices.

Mr. Speaker, if you allow me to continue I can be right there. Now I come to money supply. I am just relating the actions of these companies to the effect on our cost of living and the price increases suffered by persons generally. This amendment moved by the hon. member for Ottawa West deals with the question of the largest expansion in money supply in any year since the war and the highest bank rate since the Bank of Canada was established. I want to deal with those aspects of the amendment, Mr. Speaker.
In order to buttress my argument, I do want to quote from Mr. Reginald McKenna in the Monetary Times of April, 1959. This is a very respectable organ, I should think, from a government point of view. This is what he has to say:
History has shown that apart perhaps from wars and religious intolerance no single factor has been more productive of misery and misfortune than the high degree of variability in the general price level. This may sound like an extravagant statement, but so far from being of the nature of a demagogic outburst it is clearly demonstrable from the course of events in various countries ever since money became an important element in the life of civilized communities. A stable price level is a thing to be desired, second only to international and domestic peace.-Reginald McKenna, chairman (president of Midland Bank Ltd.).

Monetary Policy
This is a statement by Sir Josiah Stamp, and I mention this to indicate the use of this very outstanding opinion on monetary policy; I am very interested in quoting from what Sir Josiah Stamp had to say because, on one occasion, I wrote him and he sent me a copy of a book he wrote entitled, "Christianity and the Economic and Social Order". This is what Sir Josiah Stamp had to say:
When I have said quite seriously, as I have done on a number of occasions, that the problem of price level is the most important single problem of our age, I have been accused either of exaggeration or flippancy. What about trade depression in the basic industries, unemployment, labour unrest, class hatred, high taxation and the rest. My answer is that the problem of the price level is fundamental to a solution of them all.
This matter has been of great interest lately in the United States. I want to quote from the Congressional Record of February 26 of this year. There was a long debate on this question, but I shall read only from one or two statements. This is a speech by the Hon. Chester Bowles in the house of representatives, and at one point he says:
But one point, at least, is clear: If we are to succeed in our efforts to secure peace in the world and prosperity for our own people, we cannot afford to wait for the least likely development of all-for the problems themselves to grow smaller. Instead both we and our economy must grow to meet them.
Then he goes on to say:
These men have honestly convinced themselves that the American people and their congress must choose between rapid growth with inflation on the one hand or minimal growth with stable prices and some unemployment on the other.
These are the persons advocating a classical approach to inflation. Then, he continues:
-I deeply believe that those among us who assume that we must accept a slow rate of expansion with some unemployment as the best means of preventing inflation, are gravely misjudging the problems which we face.
He goes on to criticize the whole approach and to suggest some regulation of the monetary system and of the economy, although somewhat limited in its extent. We all know, that former President Lincoln made some strong statements concerning monetary policy and the purpose and place of money in our society. He said on one occasion:
To what extent has the government a responsibility to protect the currency of the nation?
Money is the creature of law and the creation of the original issue of money should be maintained as an exclusive monopoly of national government.
The monetary needs of increasing numbers of people advancing toward higher standards of living can and should be met by the government. The circulation of a medium of exchange issued and backed by the government can be properly regulated and redundancy of issue avoided by withdrawing from circulation such amounts as may be necessary by taxation, re-deposit and otherwise.

The privilege of creating and issuing money is not only the supreme prerogative of government, but it is the government's greatest creative opportunity.
Then, I want to mention again the words of a former prime minister, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King who said:
Until the control and issue of money is restored to the government, and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile.
We in this group, Mr. Speaker, certainly support this statement, as we have in the past. In our opinion the present situation provides the government with a creative opportunity. We in this group suggest the necessity for a planned national development policy, but at the same time we recognize the fact that the natural resources are under the jurisdiction of the provinces, and the fact that co-operation with the provinces in a program of this type is essential. We believe that is absolutely the first essential with respect to overcoming the situation we are faced with at the present time. We believe the federal government should give leadership in that direction.
Then we believe it is necessary to have a planned fiscal policy. In this connection we believe a national development plan and the accumulation of capital for this purpose should be established. Capital could be provided by bond issues, by obtaining the savings of the people, and this is completely non-inflationary. It is a matter that will have to be explored by this government to its ultimate possibilities and limits.
What has been done to secure the co-operation of the people of this country in support of a national development policy by lending their moneys themselves for projects for which they would be directly concerned? In that connection I think it would be a good idea to appeal to people's local loyalty. You could have a national loan for the South Saskatchewan dam, a national loan for maritime dams, or for maritime development. We have not started to mobilize the resources or to attract the interest of the Canadian people in this direction. We could secure some capital by taxing where appropriate-this is not inflationary-toward a development policy, and we could use national credit through the Bank of Canada under circumstances that will not create inflation. In order not to create inflation it must be directly related to a planned economic policy and to the rate of production.
As socialists we urge the government to consider our common sense proposals which have been proven by experience. We are not just getting up here and talking Utopian nonsense from the government members' point of view, or a lot of tommyrot. The

ideas we are expounding and do expound from time to time with respect to these problems have been proved by experience.
In this connection I want to bring to the attention of hon. members a book entitled: "Norway The Planned Revival", written by Miss Alice Bourneuf. I read this book with great interest, and I recommend it to the members of the house. I may say I was led to search into this problem by my great admiration for the Norwegians both in peace and in war, and I have friends who are Norwegians. I am one of those who recognizes that they have made a great contribution to Canadian development. I have always looked upon the Norwegians as Englishmen who failed to come over from Norway with their brothers to Britain prior to the Roman invasion. I want to bring this to the attention of the house, and to read briefly from the cover blurb:
Her emphasis is on the over-all national accounts aspect of the plans-the program for total investment, private and public consumption, output increases, and import surpluses to be financed with aid or credits. And since monetary, fiscal, and wage-price policies were an important part of Norwegian economic planning, the book devotes considerable time to an analysis of the stabilization program-
This is the sort of program we are suggesting the government should undertake at the present time. I continue:
-the gradual easing of inflationary pressures, the importance of high public savings, and the measures which led to a very high rate of private savings. Also discussed in detail is the problem of maintaining some degree of price-wage stability in spite of rapidly rising import prices, the 1949 devaluation, over-full employment, and a domestic price and wage level held down by means of subsidies and price controls.
Norway's experience is important not only in and for itself, but as a pilot study for other countries engaged in economic planning.
I bring this to the attention of the Minister of Finance. I would like to see him give some consideration to the outline in this book of the policies of the Norwegian government, which is a labour government, a democratic socialist government that has been engaged in socialist planning and the maintenance of real freedom both i<n the economic and political spheres. In this connection I want to read a short paragraph or two from this book. From page 210 I read this:
One obvious fact is that Norway eliminated inflationary pressures in the consumer section only by a strong combination of fiscal policy, price-wage policy, and policy on the use of resources for consumption. The heavy reliance on fiscal and price-wage policies to keep the controlled price system from getting too far out of line with disposable incomes, and gradually to bring it more into line, was of the utmost importance. Fiscal and wage policies are less manageable in many countries.

They did that through the co-operation of business itself. They established a committee representing government, industry, labour and the farmers, as I said, to suggest means of controlling the price-wage spiral. I quote:
The report strongly advocates the establishment of a permanent co-operation council to watch Norwegian economic developments and to offer such proposals as it might deem necessary.
Moreover, efforts should be made to co-ordinate price and wage negotiations through a co-operation council in which the government, wage-earners, employers and agriculture would be represented.
That has been the approach of the democratic socialist government of Norway, and it has met with considerable success to date. Surely we in Canada with our greater natural resources and opportunities can approach this problem along similar lines. Therefore we suggest similar planning be undertaken in Canada, with co-operation between the government, wage-earners, employers and agriculture, and as a result of that co-operation it is our opinion that we would get a stabilization of prices and wages which would be of great benefit to the working people of this country.	*

Mr. Speaker, we believe that the policy I have outlined in these brief remarks on national planning and development related to governmental control of the issue of currency, plus co-operation between the government, industry, labour and agriculture, will be a great step forward. We believe these proposals will lead toward a planned development of our resources, a stable fiscal policy, full employment and security for all Canadians. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in concluding my remarks I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier):
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following words:

Mr. Speaker, in referring to the way in which the government has handled our debt I wish first of all to refer briefly to what I consider to be the greatest financial fiasco in the history of our country, namely the conversion loan. Our people will feel the effect of this loan for a generation.
I have said previously in this house that less than 55 per cent of those bonds were in fact being extended over a longer term. Over 45 per cent of those victory bonds must again be dealt with as they have been converted into short term loans maturing in either 1961 or 1965, and both issues come due before the ninth victory loan would have come due and been ready for conversion. The 1961 loan amounting to $1 billion will need to be converted during the lifetime of this parliament, and the 1965 loan amounting to over $1.2 billion will come due in the year I have mentioned, and will need to be converted during the lifetime of the next parliament. I think we have paid a very high price in order to get just slightly over half of these bonds extended to bonds of a longer due date. We have heard all kinds of prices mentioned, and a figure of over $70 million has been named as the cost of that conversion.
At the time of the conversion, I well recall saying that I could not condone the expenditure of over $16 million for the printing bureau, especially if there was any irregularity, and none was proved. I told the minister that in extra debt charges his conversion policy would be costing the people of Canada the equivalent of one printing bureau every three months for a generation, or one almost every mile from here to Montreal. The minister told me then that I was irresponsible. Well, let us see how irresponsible I was. Including the cost of the loan-over $70 million -and the extra interest, the minister, had he been building printing bureaux, would, starting at Eastview, have completed four, with another four nearing completion. By the fall he would be starting work on four more, and be 12 miles out of the city toward Montreal with 23 years yet to go. And this would represent only part of the cost, because
Monetary Policy
on the other side of the road he would also have as many other imposing structures, progressively more ornate as you go east representing the extra interest our people have to pay for provincial, municipal and other loans because of that conversion program.
Every new sidewalk, new school, new hospital, sewer or road will cost more because of that conversion loan. As an example, the city of Welland and the township of Crowland in my own county are building a new hospital; the two municipalities are underwriting a substantial share of the cost. When they come to sell debentures they will get some concept of what that conversion loan and the fiscal policy of this government have done to them. A good many municipalities have not built new projects since the time of the conversion loan. They will be going on the market soon to borrow money, and at that point they will speedily realize what this conversion loan and what the other activities of this government have cost the people of Canada. If we turn to table 48, page 87, of the budgetary papers it will be seen that the minister is in big business. In the last fiscal year the total amount of securities issued was $9.2 billion. Renewals or conversions amounted to $6.8 billion, and the amount issued for new cash was $2.4 billion. The trouble is that so much of the new borrowing by this government to meet deficits and other expenditures was on short term. The issues are again right on top of us to finance again in this current year and in the year which lies ahead.
The minister talked a great deal about the victory loans, amounting to $6.4 billion, overhanging the market. He has now worked himself into a position where, as will be seen from an examination of the budgetary papers, he has over $7 billion overhanging the market between now and the end of 1966 when the ninth victory bond was due-I am including the new borrowing which he must make this year to cover the deficit and other budgetary loans. This calculation does not, however, include the $1.59 billion of treasury bills which was increased by $70 million last year in order to get more cash, or new borrowings, or the deficit in succeeding years.
As I said before, the total amount of bonds issued in the last fiscal year by conversion for new cash amounted to 9.2 billion. If nearly $1.6 billion of three months treasury bills is added to this hon. members will see that the minister has been fooling around with over half our total debt, and this costs money, as is evidenced by the conversion loan itself. Truly this government's greed for cash is insatiable. In spite of their promises, they had to get more money.

Monetary Policy
The minister has told us that as far as he can judge the Canadian public has been well informed about the situation with regard to our debt and the money we have to raise. Well, the overspending in deficits and the depletion in government accounts amount to more than twice the total budget for 1939. The "moderate increase" in taxes of $352 million-and this is the only time I will refer to the budget-is 75 per cent of the total budget of 1939, with an estimated deficit amounting to some $400 million which is, itself, not far off the total 1939 budget.
This year the estimates are away up again, and there seems no end to the increase in spending. The government is taking so much of our earnings, and competing so strongly for money which the provinces, the municipalities and the school boards have to find on the open market in competition with the government to finance their legitimate needs, that the future cannot possibly be regarded with confidence. There surely must be a limit to all this. At the time of the conversion loan, the minister said one result would be that the provinces and the municipalities would be able to get money at better advantage, by which he meant at more satisfactory rates of interest. But in his last pronouncement, the minister did not go out on a limb. He merely said he wanted to leave more room for the provinces and municipalities to borrow money. I am afraid he has not left them much room unless they pay very high rates.
If the minister had sold his short term bonds at par around a rate commensurate with present yields instead of putting in income tax gimmicks costing our treasury a net 6.6 per cent when sold to corporations he would have a more stable market. Bond buyers are holding back in full knowledge of the number of bonds the minister must finance, waiting to see what gimmicks might be in store for them. Surely, the minister is directly responsible for creating an irregular and unsatisfactory bond market.
The next time the minister has a bond issue with gimmicks I think he should make the bonds available in smaller denominations to the small businessmen. The last bonds were sold in denominations of $1,000, $5,000, $100,000 and $1 million. The small businessmen might as well get in on the benefits at this time because they will be shown no discrimination when the bill is to be paid. The next bond issue should not be handled on the basis of a 15-minute rush. As the minister said, at the time of the last loan the books were opened and closed in 15 minutes. Certainly the ordinary man did not

get much chance to get a bond even if he had $1,000, the amount of the lowest denomination.
At any time I have heard the minister speak in the budget debate or on any other occasion he has nearly always justified the high interest rates in Canada on the basis of those in the United States. Let us review what has been done in that country. There were three issues in the United States sold immediately prior to our conversion loan bond issue. They were in May and June of 1958. The United States treasury sold $1 billion worth of bonds representing only one-third of 1 per cent of their total debt in 27-year 3-J per cent bonds slightly above par. They were 50 cents for each $100 above par. There was so much criticism of the United States treasury over this high interest rate of 3J per cent that the treasury went into shorter term bonds. On June 15, 1958 they had to refund $9.5 billion of notes and bonds coming due. They did this in two parcels which I will describe. They floated $1.8 billion in 11-month 1J per cent certificates. The larger one involved the sum of $7.4 billion which was floated in 6-year 8-month bonds to yield 2.58 per cent. They were doing this at a time when we were getting rid of the 8th and 9th series of bonds. At the corresponding time they sold new bonds to return to the buyer 2.58 per cent. These were sold to the public at 50 cents per $100 above par. The whole issue was sold and this left $356 million that had to be redeemed for cash. The point is that our 4i per cent bonds were 1J per cent in yield over the comparatively small amount sold by the United States treasury at 3J per cent and for which they were severely criticized, and If or nearly 2 per cent over the larger United States 2f per cent issue.
It is true that United States short term money is up; in fact, the figure of 4 per cent was mentioned in today's Globe and Mail. It may be pointed out, however, that our last short term 13-month loan sold in February, with its income tax gimmicks, cost our government 6.6 per cent net when sold to big corporations. This is still considerably more than 2 per cent over United States short term loans. We surely want to keep ahead of the United States.
One bad feature in connection with our borrowings is the lack of stability on the part of the Department of Finance. Most of our bonds were selling on the market to yield slightly under 5 per cent and then the minister offered $200 million of bonds in two issues, both of which carried income tax gimmicks. As I said before the shorter term 13-month bonds because of the income tax gimmicks returned 6.6 per cent. This is

bad in itself but there is another bad aspect of this. Because of these sudden upward jumps in interest rates the people who have money to invest in the bond market are sitting back waiting to see if any new income tax gimmicks might come their way. No one buying a bond returning a high interest rate wants to see his bond go down as a result of the Department of Finance offering a bond at a higher interest rate. Many of the bond buyers are afraid of this. Both the man buying a $50 bond and the man buying a $1 million bond do not want to see their bonds go down in price next month.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, nobody in this country can deny that we are approaching or are in some form of financial crisis. Last Thursday I asked the Minister of Finance this question, as found at page 2968 of Hansard:
Is it true that the new treasury bill rate is now 4.72 per cent, and that the bank rate has reached another unprecedented record high of close to 5 per cent?
His answer was:
I have not the precise figure for this week's rates, but I would say that the movement in the rate on treasury bills lately has been attributable directly to the tremendous demands for commercial loans which are being made at this time on the chartered banks, reflecting the very great expansion in the economy of this country which is under way at present.
I would say that these rate increases were depressing financial news to the people of the country. The minister evidently did not know how many percentage points rise had occurred in the treasury bill rate. This rate sets the bank rate which is .25 above it, and it also in effect sets the commercial rate which now stands at 5} per cent. These rates have a tremendous effect on the business tempo in our country.
I realize that there has been some industrial pick-up, I think about two points, but if it is to be sustained and if it is to progress we must have money at reasonable rates in order that it may do so. If there ever was a time when a pick-up of the business tempo was needed it is now because we have so many people unemployed. Yet the minister did not know what the interest rates were at a time when later that day and the following morning they made headline news in the papers across our country. The minister should do all he can to stimulate an industrial pick-up. The time has come when the minister should take
Monetary Policy
the people of Canada into his confidence. They have the right to expect honest and straightforward statements as to our fiscal policy and not misleading ones such as have been given by the minister, three examples of which I referred to in the budget debate.
Nothing will precipitate a crisis faster than lack of candour on the part of the minister. Doubt is worse than reality. In February, as you know, our short term bonds were sold, as I said before, on a basis actually costing the government 6.6 per cent but most of our bonds were selling on the Canadian market to yield between 4.75 and 5 per cent. I think there must be something seriously wrong with our fiscal policy when the Minister of Finance finds it necessary to put out bonds at such a high rate and such a high cost to the government of our country. I said before that our money was costing us more and therefore our bonds are selling lower than bonds of most countries of the western free world.
Federal government borrowings are the senior security in our country. In my lifetime they have always been considered to be the best and safest investment and they have always sold to give a lower yield than provincial and municipal bonds. This is not so today because many equivalent maturities of most provincial and provincial guaranteed bonds are selling either on a par with, or slightly above Canadian government bonds. I said in the speech from the throne debate that the minister would soon be competing with our cities, towns, and townships for money, and that has come about at the present time. Even at present many of our fellow Canadians are willing to buy some of these debentures ahead of the senior maturities of our country and I know that some of our municipalities do not have to pay 6.6 per cent. They get their money cheaper than that.
Why is this so? It has never been the case in our country that municipalities have been able to obtain money as cheaply as the Dominion of Canada. The reason must be that many investors have greater faith in municipal councils and the way they manage their affairs. This has occurred only during the time that the present minister has been in office.
The Conservative party has never been outstanding in their handling of financial matters in Canada. Only twice since confederation have they had a surplus of more than $1 million, once in this century and once in the last century. It is true that they had two other surpluses but they were both less than $1 million. Altogether their past surpluses did not amount to over $15 million,

Monetary Policy
and the government has been overspending by that amount in every week of the last fiscal year.
After all, what can we expect? The government has no fiscal policy. It has no long term or short term fiscal policy. They go along day by day and I think their consciences are plagued by their promises. They deal with financial problems one at a time but unfortunately debt, deficits and poor financing are not easily dismissed. They stay to plague them. I know that the firing of a sub-postmaster and the firing of a lot of men who worked on the Arrow project are matters that the government hopes the people will soon forget but certainly their fiscal policy stays with them and it has become a nightmare.
I am not going to refer extensively to what the minister said in the budget debate, but as found at page 2889 of Hansard of April 21, 1959 the minister did say this:
If we had been elected earlier unquestionably we could have saved this country money by eliminating waste and extravagance.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I say at this point that it seems to me that the hon. member is reverting to the budget debate rather than dealing with the question before us.

I will not do so further ex-cep't to quote one sentence with reference to capital. I was really glad to hear the minister say this in the budget debate. The minister said: "Capital in this country is not unlimited." I think that refers to something we are debating. He also said:
Our policy has been, as hon. members know, to resist as far as lies within our power the payment of high interest rates on federal borrowings.
For the life of me I cannot understand that statement after the conversion loan fiasco and after the loans at 6.6 per cent with respect to which the bonds were sold, as I said before, to corporations, most of whom would be paying 50 per cent or more income tax. I think it is over 50 per cent now when you take in the old age pension part of it. When the minister gets into trouble he seems to blame the United States but I have already put on the record today some facts as to how the United States has handled its loans. I think I put on the record here today that the United States, certainly before the conversion loan, was able to obtain money cheaper, often up to 2 per cent.
There was no mention by the minister of the British budget. I do not suppose I should mention the British budget, but this year Britain was able to grant tax reductions amounting to about $1 billion, with an indicated surplus of $102 million.

One reason back of our trouble in this country is the lack of foreign investment. It is certainly not coming into the country as fast as it used to come. One reason for this is the anti-Americanism which was created in this country and stirred up on many Tory platforms and by some of the Tory press. It certainly was so in my part of the country. I saw in the newspapers a story about a broker from Montreal who said he used to have a lot of Canadian bond buyers from the United States, but since the conversion loan he has not had any. I have cited before in this house how unpopular our bonds are in New York. I refer to the fact that one week one lone Canadian $1,000 bond was sold on the New York market during a week as against $375,000 worth of Australian bonds. During the week following that, not one Canadian bond was sold, while practically the same number of Australian bonds were sold. I know a few Canadians personally who used to buy our bonds but now they not only do not buy our bonds but they have sold the ones they bought at a loss.
Even the unemployment insurance commission fund, over which the minister has control, I understand took a loss of $10,115,171.51 in the government bonds they had to sell within the last year. I am surprised that the minister would be forced to take such a loss in one of the government accounts. I am often asked by people from the United States when I meet them, "What kind of government have you in Canada, anyhow?" I can only reply in the words used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) when he was asked in Chicago about the diversion of trade and the anti-Americanism he said, "That was only election talk". Unfortunately, the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce do not catch up with the publicity in the United States press emanating from Ottawa about the diversion of 15 per cent of the trade and the criticism of United States investments in Canada. The average citizen of the United States, therefore, who might help us by buying bonds or who might invest some money in Canada, does not do so. He merely asks, "What kind of government have you in Canada, anyhow?" Even I wonder. After all this anti-Americanism, after all the great pronouncements by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) about maintaining our sovereignty in Canada our government leases oil and gas rights on three million acres to corporations, 90 per cent of which were either United States corporations or United States controlled.
The press has referred to this time in our history as a strange interlude, as being unpredictable and not knowing where we are

going. Certainly, this government is strange and their actions seem to be stranger than fiction. I hear the minister is going to the Department of External Affairs. I wish him well, and I would say that the department is badly in need of a head at the present time. I think the minister will do well there because lately he has demonstrated more tact and patience than I thought was possible. In my opinion, he has many admirable qualities and accomplishments, although I do not believe mathematics is one of them. I congratulate the minister upon his work and his industry, but I regret that our fiscal policy is in such a mess that our Prime Minister feels it is necessary to move him.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that many of the mayors and aldermen of the municipalities of Canada were shocked when they read in the newspapers over the week end that in the future the rate of interest for money would be 5} per cent. Municipal debentures at 5 J or 5| per cent will cripple the Canadian municipalities and discourage the undertaking of public works throughout the whole of Canada. A $2 million debenture at 5| per cent would cost a municipality $115,000 a year in interest alone. If the population were approximately 9,000 in that municipality, the cost per year for interest charges only would amount to $12.78 per person or $63.90 per year for an average family of five. A municipality with a total taxable valuation of $25 million would have to collect from the proprietor of an immovable valued at $20,000 an annual tax of $92 for interest alone. This amount would be over and above the ordinary taxes levied.
If the ordinary municipal tax imposed on this property were $360, adding $92 would raise the taxes to $452, an increase of 25.5 per cent. At the present time it is very difficult to borrow money at less than 5i or 5J per cent. I have here a clipping from a newspaper in which the city of Kitchener is inviting tenders for debentures and the maturity rates are 5J per cent, one to ten years; 5i per cent, one to fifteen years, and 5J per cent, one to fifteen years. In one of the latest booklets issued by a broker in Montreal it is indicated that the rate of interest for municipal hospital and school debentures is 5 to 5j per cent.
Now an interest rate of 5} per cent is the highest rate in recent years. It was at this rate in August, 1957 and it dropped to 5J per cent in February, 1958. It rose to 5J per cent in March, 1959 and at the end of this April it rose again to 5f per cent. Now the increase in the cost of wages and salaries, as a result of the increased cost of living,
Monetary Policy
plus the higher cost of the necessary equipment, placed the municipalities of Canada in a very difficult situation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; the hon. member seems to be addressing his remarks to the problem of interest on municipal borrowings. There is no mention of that in the amendment before the house, and I should like to remind him that on the first supply motion during this session a subamendment called for consideration at a conference of such federal proposals to reduce the burden of interest rates on new provincial and municipal borrowings, which subamendment was negatived by the house. I wonder if I might speak to the point Your Honour has just made. The governing part of the amendment before the house is what I would think should really be discussed at this time. It reads as follows:
This house regrets the ill-conceived and irresponsible actions of the government in the field of debt management and monetary policy-
Points 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 are descriptive only and are by no means all inclusive of the effects of the government's debt management and monetary policy.
What the hon. gentleman is seeking to do is quite obviously, I submit with great respect, to show that as a result of the government's debt management and monetary policies municipal financing has been rendered more difficult. With regard to the specific characteristic in No. 2, it should be noted that the bank rate does not preclude a discussion of the matter of interest rates, I submit, within the proper context of the question because the highest bank rate is not what we mean by interest rate. The bank rate is something which may have a determining factor on what the interest rate is but by itself it is not to be regarded as meaning the same thing as the interest rate.
I would submit with respect that the hon. gentleman deserves the latitude he is seeking because he is seeking to show that the situation confronting municipal financing is the product of the government's monetary policy and debt management.

Monetary Policy

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I say this with respect to what the hon. member for Essex East has submitted? If the amendment had simply the first paragraph it would scarcely have been admissible because the term "monetary policy" is too broad, and would take us back over the ground of the budget debate which we have just finished. Therefore I regard the amendment, which deals with debt management and monetary policy, to be limited by the five specific items which follows; otherwise it seems to me that it overlaps a good part of what has been discussed in other debates during this session. Therefore I feel that the discussion should be restricted to the specific items one to five which are specified as the aspects of debt management and monetary policy which the house is to discuss.
Now with respect to the line which has been taken by the hon. member for Outre-mont-St. Jean. He goes directly over ground which has been debated in the house, and that is the reason why I felt in discussing municipal and provincial finances, and this government's attitude towards the problem, he Was repeating a previous debate, and more properly should have made his speech at that time rather than this time. I do not feel that I should allow a wide range of debate on the amendment before the house.

Would Your Honour hear another word on this point? It seems to me that the governing word in the motion moved by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) is the verb "regrets". The house is asked to regret what we on this side of the house feel to have been the ill-conceived and irresponsible actions of the government in the field of debt management and monetary policy. It seems to me that this is quite different from the motion that was decided by the house earlier. The house was asked earlier to take some specific action about this interest; but I apprehend that my hon. friend is not asking the house to take any specific course of action but to express regret about the subject, and he has given his reason why we should regret that. All of us have our own reasons for regretting it.
The last election.

A rate of 5| per cent is going to be a very serious handicap to all of these organizations. In my municipality, if I may say so, in 1947, we paid $515,568 in wages, and now in 1959 we are paying-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope the hon. member did not misunderstand me. I have not accepted the proposition which has been made that we can go into a discussion of municipal and provincial debt. This interest of 5} per cent is going to have a serious effect on employment in the province of Quebec because municipalities and all of these other organizations borrow to create work and to build. On March 22, 1958 we had 222,000 unemployed in the province of Quebec. On March 21, 1959 we had 215,000. The stockbrokers and investment houses will certainly suffer from this high rate of interest. It is going to place a heavy burden on their shoulders, and I am sure the number of investors will become fewer and fewer as time goes on.
This high rate of interest will curtail the exports of Canadian goods, and it will add to the cost of manufacture. oil in April has fallen to around 300,000 barrels a day, after being in excess of 400,000 barrels during the first two months of the year.
I have a lot of statistics, but in deference to your ruling, I suppose I had better let them go. That will be all.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Yes.

If the hon. gentleman has that regret, why does he not fill that vacuum?
Monetary Policy
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) is a sharp enough observer in this house to realize very well indeed that our subamendment was ruled out of order.

That does not preclude
another.

Therefore our proposals as to a remedy may not be debated at this time. However, to get back to the Conservatives, as I indicated before, since 1935 they have learned nothing; hence the reason for the complaints at the present time.
The over-all approach which I can only assume is being taken by the Conservative government at this time is that matters will right themselves. I regret that my colleague, the member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), had to file his documents with the Hansard office a little while ago and I therefore have not with me the copy of the speech rendered to the house of representatives in Washington by the Honourable Chester Bowles, where he warned in unmistakable terms that if we are going to adopt the philosophy that our problems will resolve themselves, we are headed for serious trouble indeed. I imagine that applies in the United States of America equally as well as here in Canada. The only way out of our difficulties is for the government to see the problems and to resolve upon a course of action. It is our contention that almost any plan of action would be preferable to lack of action and to a philosophy of letting sleeping dogs lie and matters will adjust themselves.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to review the complaints that we note in the amendment. I see that the first one is a complaint that the government's policy in regard to management of debt and monetary matters has been characterized by errors and inequities associated with the conversion loan. Our complaint about the conversion loan is, first of all, that the rate of interest offered was needlessly high. As evidence we call attention to the activities on the money markets of Canada. If the rate which had been offered had been realistic at the time and in line with market conditions, government of Canada bonds would not have suddenly leaped ahead as they did, especially victory bonds.
Our next complaint on the conversion loan is that with regard to the new bonds which have been issued-I have particular reference now to the 4J per cent, 25-year bonds- they were non-callable. We feel that action was most irresponsible. We also complain that the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) appeared on a

Monetary Policy
add to the tax burden of every Canadian. The action-and more especially the lack of action-on the part of this government will cause municipal and provincial taxes to rise and will, as the minister admitted in the budget, cause an increase in federal taxes. It will mean in effect that our municipalities and provinces will be unable to take action concerning much needed services and activities of this nature will of necessity be curtailed.
One of the most shameful things that has happened in Canada took place about a month ago when the old age pensioners were blamed for tax increases. I believe that the monetary policies of this government rather than the old age pensioners are to be blamed. High interest rates result in increased costs of production and make worse the cost-price squeeze. At this time when we are particularly concerned about unemployment I regret that the actions and the lack of action on the part of this government in the field of monetary policy generally and specifically with respect to interest charges is causing a slowdown of the industrial development of Canada. When you think of automation especially you will realize the important relationship this has to the ever-increasing number of unemployed from one end of the country to the other. When industrial enterprises are faced with high carrying charges and capital costs there is a tendency to delay and postpone any planned industrial expansion that may have been contemplated and jobs that might have been provided to the unemployed do not come into existence.
We also regret the influence that the policies of the government have on the buying power of the average Canadian. This has a tremendous effect on the home market which is, after all, our most important market. When you take away from the purchasing power of the people in order to meet these high interest charges you interfere with the ability of Canadians to provide themselves with the necessities of life.
The Liberals in this house have complained that the actions of the government were wrong and we in this group agree that the little action the government has taken to meet the problems of the day has been unwise, especially in relation to monetary policy and more specifically in relation to interest charges. The government follows a policy of sitting it out, waiting it out and letting problems resolve themselves. We regret that the only action the government will see fit to take will be in the application of the outmoded Tory policies of the hungry thirties.
In the main, however, we complain about the lack of policy which we contend might be

remedied by this parliament assuming control of the currency and credit of the nation. I know that the Prime Minister is a westerner. I only wish that at an early date we would have the announcement of the appointment of a new secretary of state for external affairs. While the knowledge of the Prime Minister with respect to economics may be weak I have sufficient confidence in him as a westerner to entertain some hope that he may be amenable to the advice of modern economists. I would like to see him seize the responsibility that is his and aid the people of Canada by implementing our proposal that this parliament must assume complete responsibility for the issuance of all currency, for the control of all credit and more specifically for the early establishment of a national investment board in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say I feel deeply flattered by the compliment that was paid today by the Liberal opposition in renewing to all intents and purposes the budget debate. I sat through the budget debate for eight days. I inflicted upon the house a very long speech to begin with and then last Tuesday inflicted upon the house a rather long reply to the Liberal amendment. Now they are back again today extending in effect the budget debate and I am afraid the house will have to submit to a speech from me on this third occasion.
We have in effect seen here an extension of the budget debate today, Mr. Speaker, because while I will not renew the argument that was addressed to you on the subject of whether the amendment was in order I will point out that everything that has been said today has touched on something that was said at one time or another during the budget debate, and something that relates to matters that the house must concern itself with in any budget debate. Indeed, the speeches have abounded with references, direct or indirect, to the budget and to things that were said in the course of the budget debate.
As I have on other occasions, Mr. Speaker, I express regret at the utter absence on the part of the official opposition of anything constructive in their approach to the matters they discussed today. They have not put forward one single constructive idea in this debate. There have been plenty, of course, that were destructive. They were under no inhibitions or restraints or restrictions in the things they had to say that pilloried the credit of Canada. Apparently the responsibility which they bear as members of parliament in

discussing matters that mean a great deal to the welfare of Canada is something that is of small concern to them. I will say this for the C.C.F., that at least they tried to put forward some ideas. However mistaken, however misjudged, however wrong those ideas were, they at least tried to put forward their ideas, but from the official opposition we have yet to hear one single inkling of how they would approach these problems.
They have talked about the problems, as was the case in the debate that ended last week. They have magnified and exaggerated the problems out of all recognition, but never once did they allow to escape from their lips a single constructive utterance or inkling or suggestion of how they would approach these problems. We will look in vain to that quarter for any suggestion as to how these problems should be met.
I am rising on a point of order. I submit to Your Honour that there is a rule of the house against tedious repetition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, no member of the house should know that rule better than the hon. gentleman because no one breaks it more than he does.
I am not tedious.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So, Mr. Speaker, I dismiss this latest interruption from the talkative member by quoting the words of scripture, "Physician, heal thyself".
The hon. gentleman would not say my speeches were tedious.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If I said they were only tedious I would be more than generous and polite to him. So, Mr. Speaker, I say in review that this kind of performance on the part of the official opposition is not a responsible performance in this house. When they can, by their tactics of exaggeration, make any problem that Canada faces today look grim, how happy they are. Indeed, they are not happy until they exaggerate these problems beyond recognition.
There is nothing that has been said today thus far that is going to help Canada's credit. There is not one thing that has been said by a member of the opposition in this debate that is going to help Canada meet her financial problems on better terms or to improve in any respect Canada's position. Such is the test of the performance by hon. members opposite.
It is regrettable that, whether by calculated design or accident or their failure to grasp the problem, they have a confused approach to these questions. I do not pretend for one minute that I shall be able to assist them out
Monetary Policy
of their confusion but in my remarks in the course of this debate I shall try as best I can to set the record straight and remove some of the error and confusion and clouding of issues that have been caused by hon. members of the opposition opposite.
It is no secret that a government must have money. Governments have no secret source of money. They must turn to the people for it. There is no magic source available to governments. What are the sources open to governments that need cash? They can raise it by taxation, they can raise it by borrowing or they can, if they were so disposed, create money by turning loose the printing presses.
I do not need to say to the house that the government has no intention whatever now or any other time, I take it, of debauching the currency of the country by resorting to the printing press. Such things have been advocated in the house in past years, but it is no part of our approach to financial problems to resort to that kind of destructive expedient. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we are faced with the necessity of finding money for the necessary purposes of government, either by taxation or by borrowing.
The borrowings of the government of Canada take several forms. First of all, there are treasury bills which are issued each week. The government invites tenders each week for a stipulated amount of money and, according to our current practice, these treasury bills expire in 91 days. In the United States they have treasury bills of various maturities. Our practice in this country in recent years has been to issue treasury bills for the uniform period of 91 days. We also issue bonds and, without trying to draw exact lines, bonds are classified in the market according to those of short duration, medium and long, and, of course, the approach to each of these classes of maturities is governed by the return involved. Very often we find a measurable difference in return in these various classes of maturities. The market at any one time may favour one class of government obligation as against another or others and from time to time there will be a shift in the public reception of the different classes of offerings.
I think I should begin this reply, Mr. Speaker, by a reference to what actually has occurred in the money market of Canada. We have had a money market in this country now for approximately the last four years. Money markets are not greatly different from commodity markets in this respect, that they are governed, not entirely but very largely, by the law of supply and demand. Obviously if the

Monetary Policy
demand is large in relation to supply the return on borrowings must be larger because the earning power of money is greater. Alternatively, when the supply is large in relation to demand, the earning power of money will be reduced and borrowing can then be had at lower rates of interest. Interest is simply a means we have of measuring the value of money as a return on the use of it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us put some facts straight at the outset. We are told here in this house that the rates that the government of Canada must pay on borrowings have been rising and, indeed, have reached record proportions. It is one thing to talk about treasury bills, and it is another thing to talk in generalities. Hon. members opposite today, when they have launched out on the subject of treasury bill rates, have either confused themselves or by typical sophistry jumped into an area of generalities from that point concerning interest rates in general. We should put some facts straight. It is true that last Thursday the Bank of Canada rate reached a record 4.97 per cent. This is somewhat larger than the rate was about 20 months ago.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that in the year 1957, before we came into office, interest rates were moving up. Indeed, from 1955 forward interest rates in general were moving upwards. This is not a phenomenon that has suddenly emerged since June 21, 1957, and attempts by speakers to leave that impression of course are not only nonsensical but they are contrary to fact. Effective interest rates began to rise in this country measurably in 1955; they were rising steadily in the early part of 1957. It was only after the new government had been in office about two months that the change came about and interest rates then began to recede. Interest rates, from that point on, dropped steadily. I am speaking now particularly of the treasury bill rate and the Bank of Canada rate associated with it. These rates dropped steadily until the spring of 1958, and then in 1958 the treasury bill rate began to rise again.
While there were fluctuations up and down, the interest rate today on treasury bills is higher than it has been in these past times. It is not a great deal higher than it was in the summer of 1957, but it is admittedly higher. Let us look at some of these figures, Mr. Speaker. On the three-month treasury bills, the rate in the summer of 1957, August, was 4.08; at the end of 1957, the rate had dropped to 3.60.

I wonder if the minister would permit a question on that figure? I have the Bank of Canada statistical summary before me, and the rates seem to be a little different. I wonder if he would give me the statistical authority? I am not questioning his figure, but I should like to have the same one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member should be aware of the fact that the treasury bill rate as reported on page 111 of the statistical summary of the Bank of Canada for March, 1959 selects the weekly rate for the last week of the month. Now the weekly rate for the last week of the month of August, which was August 28 of that year, was 4.03 per cent, but the rate during that month reached 4.08 per cent.
By December 31, 1957, the rate as I have indicated had dropped to 3.60 per cent; by April 21, 1958 it had dropped to 1.37 and it reached its low in July, 1958, when the rate dropped to .87 per cent, the lowest for years, a rate of less than 1 per cent. Then, as I have indicated, a rise began in the late summer of 1958, and the rate has moved up gradually, just as it did in the United States. We have a rate on November 19, 1958 of 3 per cent; December 31, 1958, 3.49 per cent; and on April 24, 1959, 4.72 per cent. This is the treasury bill rate.
Now, Mr. Speaker, hon. members opposite have chosen, without any more factual basis than that, to picture this country as going to the bow-wows, as though we were heading straight for a crisis. Let us see this matter in its true proportions. No minister of finance, no government enjoys paying any more for the money it has to borrow than it must pay. Believe me, there is no pleasure in paying high interest rates. The fact is that these are weekly offerings. The treasury bill rate is the most volatile rate amongst all government obligations, and the fluctuations in the rate can at least be understood in relation to this fact, which has some comfort in it, that these rates exist for only three months. When reductions occur, the reductions in rate are quickly felt and the government is in a position to take immediate advantage of them because they are weekly offerings.
What are some of the other movements in interest rates? We have been told here today that the country is going to perdition because the chartered bank prime rate has risen, as of today, to 5J per cent. Mr. Speaker, again let us, while not taking any satisfaction out of the fact that this rate has gone up, see this in its true relationship. This rate has gone back to what it was in the summer of 1957.
What did you say about it then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I had this to say, that we inherited a situation from our predecessors, who were very generous in bequeathing problems to us that they did not have either the courage or competence to handle.
More tedious repetition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You would think from their talking today that a rise in interest rates had never occurred before. Let us look at what happened in the regime of these gentlemen who are so boastful today. Let us just go back to 1945. These figures that
1	give now are the prime interest rate charged by the chartered banks of Canada.
From 1945 to April 23, 1956 the rate was 4J per cent. On April 23, 1956 it was moved up to 5 per cent. On August 20, 1956 it was moved up to 5J per cent. On October 22, 1956 it was moved up to 51 per cent. On August 26, 1957 it was moved up to 5f per cent. On December 2, 1957 it went down to 51 per cent. On February 17, 1958 it went down to 51 per cent. On March 8, 1959 it went up to 51 per cent. On April 27 it went up to 5f per cent.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, seen in the light of these figures, while we may not like it- and I do not suppose any of us do like to see this present rise in interest rates-the fact is that it is a rise that brings us back to the figure that was reached over 20 months ago, and that following that, through the late part of 1957 and the first half of 1958, the rate went down. This is a rate that has fluctuated frequently according to conditions.
We are told it is deplorable that the Bank of Canada rate should have risen. The Bank of Canada sometime ago chose to set its rate in terms of a formula attached to the treasury bill rate. This was not always the case. For years the Bank of Canada set a rate. That rate stood at 2 per cent from October, 1950 to February 14, 1955. It was then reduced to 11 per cent. It was raised to
2	per cent on August 5, 1955; to 2i per
cent on October 12, 1955; to 2f per cent on November 18,	1955; to 3 per cent on
April 4, 1956; to 3| per cent on August 9, 1956; and to 31 per cent on October 17, 1956.
Now, Mr. Speaker, will you note that in the days when hon. members opposite were in power the rate set by the Bank of Canada advanced from 11 per cent in February, 1955 to 31 per cent in October, 1956. In other words, the treasury bill rate rose by 2 per cent within a space of some 20 months. It advanced from 11 per cent to 31 per cent, a rise, if you want to measure it in percentage terms, of 133 per cent in terms of
Monetary Policy
the rate prevailing in February, 1955. That was the extent of the rise in the treasury bill rate before we came into office while the rate was still set by the Bank of Canada without reference to the treasury bill rates.
Then, the Bank of Canada, on November 1, 1956 set its rates in terms of a formula attached to the treasury bill rate. In other words, from that point on the Bank of Canada did not attempt to set on its own account the rate on its loans. It simply accepted week by week the treasury bill rate and added a quarter of 1 per cent to it. That was the decision of the Bank of Canada. Whether the government of that day or the minister of finance of that day expressed any opinion on that subject outside the house, we do not know. We do know that he was chary about expressing any opinion on the subject in the house. The Bank of Canada did give its reasons for establishing its rate at that time in terms of this formula. Let us bear in mind that the government of Canada does not establish the Bank of Canada rate.
There are matters within the subject of the amendment that fall within the responsibility of government; there are things that fall within the responsibility of the Bank of Canada. The government is responsible for fiscal policy. The Bank of Canada, by an act of the parliament of Canada, is responsible for monetary policy, and this bank rate, as it is called, is set each week by the Bank of Canada in the exercise of its statutory powers.
I should like to place on Hansard simply for the information of the house, without either attacking or defending it, the reasons given by the Bank of Canada for attaching the bank rate to the treasury bill rate. I am reading now, from the press release issued by the Bank of Canada on November 1, 1956:
The Bank of Canada announced today that it was carrying a step further the policy announced in February 1955 of making its bank rate more flexible and responsive to changing conditions in the short-term money market. Henceforth and until further notice the bank rate, which is the minimum rate at which the central bank is prepared as a lender of last resort to make very short term loans to chartered banks and money market dealers will be at a fixed margin of one-quarter of one per cent above the latest weekly average tender rate for 91-day treasury bills. The average tender rates on treasury bills today was 3.34 per cent, a decline of .03 per cent as compared with a week ago. Accordingly the bank rate until next Thursday will be 3.59 per cent.
As indicated on several occasions by the bank, the bank rate is not changed arbitrarily or with a view to bringing about other interest rate changes. On the contrary, it has been desired since the development of the money market in Canada in late 1954 and early 1955 that the bank rate should be kept in line with other interest rates and should move when they do, but usually not otherwise. The present technical change in the method of setting the bank rate from week to week is

Monetary Policy
intended to clarify this relationship and remove what has evidently been a source of some public misunderstanding.
Interest rates are determined in the market by the interplay between the supply of and the demand for loanable funds. Transactions take place every day in considerable volume; .yields on marketable securities may change by small amounts from day to day, according to changes in the views of holders and of prospective buyers of various categories of securities as to the prices at which they are prepared to sell or buy. In general, interest rates have been rising for nearly two years because of a great growth in demand to borrow money, or to raise money by selling securities. The supply of money has increased, but the demand for it has grown even faster.
The bank rate has been increased from time to time in Canada as in other countries in line with this movement in market rates of interest. It would be clearly undesirable that banks and dealers should be able to borrow from the central bank at a lower cost than the yield on the most liquid form of government securities. Such an encouragement to borrowing from the central bank would be apt to induce an inflationary increase in the volume of money.
Changes in bank rate in the past two years have taken place in steps of one-quarter per cent or one-half per cent. One result of having the bank rate change by smaller amounts each week in closer touch with other short-term interest rates is that it will direct public attention more to the basic factors in the monetary situation, that is, changes in the supply of and demand for money.
Then, further down:
If at any time it appears that the treasury bill rate is not the best indicator of market conditions or if it is found that a different margin between market rates and bank rate would be more suitable, or that a change in monetary conditions should be more strikingly signalized, a change in the practice will be made and announced. For the time being, however, it is proposed, as indicated, to keep the bank rate at a fixed margin of one-quarter of one per cent above the average rate at the most recent weekly tender for government of Canada treasury bills, the rate which is made public at approximately 1 p.m. each Thursday immediately following the tender.
Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
I would like to ask the minister whether he approves of this technique followed by the Bank of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Monetary Policy
prevent longer-run tendencies based on real changes in supply and demand. On balance, the bank has been a buyer of government securities throughout the period of falling bond prices, that is, of rising interest rates.
I have read that extract with a view to placing before the house the bank's statement containing its view as to its function in relation to the movement of the interest rate and the supply of money. There has undoubtedly been a good deal of misunderstanding on the subject of the operations of the bank in this particular field, and I have read this statement at some length, because it is as far as I know the clearest and most comprehensive statement which the Bank of Canada has issued at any time as to the function which the bank performs in connection with interest rates and their fluctuations.
I spoke of the interaction in the money market which we have had in Canada since the end of 1954 of the forces of supply and demand. The demand for money is, of course, measured by the total effective borrowing from all sections of the country-borrowings, made by the federal government, provincial governments, municipal governments, business and persons-the whole gamut of borrowings in a free economy.
What are the factors which govern the supply of money? The two elements in money supply are currency in circulation and bank deposits. The bank deposits represent, of course, the total sum of money placed on deposit at any particular time with the chartered banks. The other element of money supply is currency in circulation, and the volume of currency in circulation in Canada is determined by the Bank of Canada and by the Bank of Canada alone. This is something strictly within the sphere of monetary action and this power, by the Bank of Canada Act, has been vested in the Bank of Canada. I wish to make it quite clear that the gov-vernment, as such, does not exercise control over the money supply or over the amount of money in circulation.
The powers and responsibilities of the bank have been clearly defined. The Bank of Canada Act defines them in three sections to which I should like to make reference. In section 18, subsection (3), the act provides:
The bank shall at all times make public the minimum rate at which it is prepared to make loans or advances.
That is the provision under which the bank derives its power and authority to establish the bank rate. The Bank of Canada rate is simply the minimum rate at which the Bank of Canada is prepared, as a lender of last resort, to make loans or advances.
Section 21 (1) of the act provides that the bank shall have the sole right to issue notes

payable to bearer on demand and intended for circulation in Canada, and that such notes shall be the first charge upon the assets of the bank. From this provision the Bank of Canada derives its exclusive power to issue notes and in that way to determine the volume of currency in circulation.
There have been questions as to the relationship between the Bank of Canada and the government. Section 20 (1) of the act provides as follows:
(1) The bank shall act as fiscal agent of the government of Canada without charge and, subject to the provisions of this act, by agreement, may also act as banker or fiscal agent of the government of any province.
There you have the provision under which the Bank of Canada operates as the fiscal agent of the government. And in subsection 2 there is the provision:
The bank, if and when required by the minister so to do, shall act as agent for the government of Canada in the payment of interest and principal and generally in respect of the management of the public debt of Canada.
In that respect it is clear that the function of the bank is that of agent, and that the government holds the responsibility before parliament and within the powers given to it by parliament in relation to the management of the public debt of Canada. The bank acts as the government's agent in this regard.
Perhaps I have sufficiently sketched the provisions under which the Bank of Canada operates and the respective functions of the bank and of the government in the fiscal field, in the management of the public debt and in the field of monetary action. And then there is, of course, the field where their re-ponsibilities are mingled and they act in association.
I have made these remarks at more length than I would have wished with a view to clarifying, if I may, the question of responsibility in this situation, because this amendment that has been moved today seeks to place upon the government the whole responsibility for the interest rates that exist in the market at the present time.
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we see an attempt in this amendment to say that because of the actions taken by the government in the field of debt management and monetary policy certain things have happened. Hon. members opposite are quite entitled to hold the government responsible for debt management with respect to that period during which the government has been in office, but I would point out that in the matter of monetary policy this parliament has placed the responsibility and indeed the power in the hands of the Bank of Canada.

The government does not exercise any sway in the field of monetary policy. The right to issue currency is vested exclusively in the Bank of Canada. Notwithstanding this fact, this misguided amendment seeks to hold the government responsible for all that has happened in the field of monetary action.
On the face of it this amendment is obviously quite misdirected. It was framed by someone who has not read the statutes enacted by this parliament. I shall have something to say in detail about the five elements that are set forth in the amendment, but I draw your attention, sir, to the fact that these are put forward in the amendment as illustrations of the results of government action in the field of debt management and monetary policy. If these five illustrations have no more validity than the general statement which precedes them then they will need a great deal to buttress them because they are founded upon a statement that is utterly at variance with the law enacted by this parliament.
I have said that this government will meet its responsibility in relation to the public debt of Canada. That is our responsibility and we shall face that responsibility. We are not, however, to be held responsible in a field where parliament has vested the determination of the Bank of Canada rate, under section 18 of the act, and the issuance of currency, under section 21 of the act, in the Bank of Canada.
Let us now look a little closer at these five illustrations. The first refers to the conversion loan. I shall have something to say about that, but perhaps I should leave those remarks until tomorrow because of the length of time that was spent on this subject today by several hon. members opposite.
The second paragraph of the amendment makes reference to the highest bank rate since the Bank of Canada was established. I point out to you that the government of Canada has no responsibility whatever for the establishment of the Bank of Canada rate. In pursuance of powers conferred upon it and responsibilities vested in it by the parliament
Monetary Policy
of Canada the Bank of Canada has established the bank rate.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I may be permitted to ask a question at this point. Since the bank rate is fixed in the way in which the minister has described by its relationship to the bids on treasury bills, would the minister deny that government policies have some effect on the amounts being bid for treasury bills?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if this amendment had spoken of the treasury bill rate it would have spoken about something that lies within the area of government action, but this misdirected amendment which as I have said was obviously drawn by someone who had not read the statute law enacted by this parliament does not speak of the treasury bill rate; it talks instead about the Bank of Canada rate...
Which is established by the treasury bill rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: . . .which is something over which this government has no control. The Bank of Canada has chosen to set this Bank of Canada rate by a formula based upon the treasury bill rate. If this amendment had talked about the treasury bill rate it would in my submission have been clear on this point and would have been dealing with something which is within the proper sphere of government action.

"Plus cela change, plus
c'est la meme chose."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The realm of action of the Bank of Canada in relation to treasury bill rates, as was made clear in the statement I read from the governor's report of 1956, consists of the purchase or sale of treasury bills. I wish to register that fact now and having made that comment may I call it ten o'clock and move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) the debate was adjourned.
